docs.title: Will you be the Kubernetes to My Docker?
docs.text: Will you be the Kubernetes to My Docker?. Let's get straight to this! What is container? Containers are a form of operating system virtualization. A single container might be used to run anything from a small microservice or software process to a larger application. Inside a container are all the necessary executables, binary code, libraries, and configuration files. Compared to server or machine virtualization approaches, however, containers do not contain operating system images. This makes them more lightweight and portable, with significantly less overhead. In larger application deployments, multiple containers may be deployed as one or more container clusters. Such clusters might be managed by a container orchestrator such as Kubernetes. ## The logo explains it all, isn’t it? Whole docker can be explained just by observing the logo Benefits of Containers Containers are a streamlined way to build, test, deploy, and redeploy applications on multiple environments from a developer’s local laptop to an on-premises data center and even the cloud. Benefits of containers include: - Less overhead. Containers require less system resources than traditional or hardware virtual machine environments because they don’t include operating system images. - Increased portability. Applications running in containers can be deployed easily to multiple different operating systems and hardware platforms. - More consistent operation. DevOps teams know applications in containers will run the same, regardless of where they are deployed. - Greater

docs.title: Will you be the Kubernetes to My Docker?
docs.text: Will you be the Kubernetes to My Docker?. efficiency. Containers allow applications to be more rapidly deployed, patched, or scaled. - Better application development. Containers support agile and DevOps efforts to accelerate development, test, and production cycles. Container Use Cases Common ways organizations use containers include: - “Lift and shift” existing applications into modern cloud architectures. Some organizations use containers to migrate existing applications into more modern environments. While this practice delivers some of the basic benefits of operating system virtualization, it does not offer the full benefits of a modular, container-based application architecture. - Refactor existing applications for containers. Although refactoring is much more intensive than lift-and-shift migration, it enables the full benefits of a container environment. - Develop new container-native applications. Much like refactoring, this approach unlocks the full benefits of containers. - Provide better support for microservices architectures. Distributed applications and microservices can be more easily isolated, deployed, and scaled using individual container building blocks. - Provide DevOps support for continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD). Container technology supports streamlined build, test, and deployment from the same container images. - Provide easier deployment of repetitive jobs and tasks. Containers are being deployed to support one or more similar processes, which often run in the background, such as ETL functions or batch jobs. What the heck is Kubernetes? _Definition by Kubernetes.io_ Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source system

docs.text: Will you be the Kubernetes to My Docker?. for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. Planet Scale Designed on the same principles that allows Google to run billions of containers a week, Kubernetes can scale without increasing your ops team. Never Outgrow Whether testing locally or running a global enterprise, Kubernetes flexibility grows with you to deliver your applications consistently and easily no matter how complex your need is. Run Anywhere Kubernetes is open source giving you the freedom to take advantage of on-premises, hybrid, or public cloud infrastructure, letting you effortlessly move workloads to where it matters to you. How Do Docker and Kubernetes Relate to Containers? Users involved in container environments are likely to hear about two popular tools and platforms used to build and manage containers. These are Docker and Kubernetes. Docker is a popular runtime environment used to create and build software inside containers. It uses Docker images (copy-on-write snapshots) to deploy containerized applications or software in multiple environments, from development to test and production. Docker was built on open standards and functions inside most common operating environments, including Linux, Microsoft Windows, and other on-premises or cloud-based infrastructures. Containerized applications can get complicated, however. When in production, many might require hundreds to thousands of separate containers in production. This is where container runtime environments such as Docker benefit from the use of

docs.title: Will you be the Kubernetes to My Docker?
docs.text: Will you be the Kubernetes to My Docker?. other tools to orchestrate or manage all the containers in operation. One of the most popular tools for this purpose is Kubernetes, a container orchestrator that recognizes multiple container runtime environments, including Docker. Kubernetes orchestrates the operation of multiple containers in harmony together. It manages areas like the use of underlying infrastructure resources for containerized applications such as the amount of compute, network, and storage resources required. Orchestration tools like Kubernetes make it easier to automate and scale container-based workloads for live production environments. Read the official documentation here for more: https://kubernetes.io/docs/home/ ## Stay curious!

docs.title: The Silent S in HTTPS
docs.text: The Silent S in HTTPS. Before we start to learn about what is HTTPS, let us first know the benefits: 1. HTTPS makes your website less vulnerable to cybercrimes Let’s say you have a website that brings your customers to a third-party page where they make purchases using a credit card. If your site isn’t secured with HTTPS, or it is set up incorrectly, bad actors can intercept the content of your website, then easily create the exact same payment page they can control and allow them to see and capture each credit card number your customers submit. Having to resolve customer complaints due to lax site security resulting in credit card theft could be fatal to your business. 2. Google tends to rank secure websites higher than websites without HTTPS When Google changed its algorithm back in 2014, we saw a 60–70% increase in SSL update among millions of websites out there. Websites that become HTTPS secure got ranked higher, while the ranking of websites without HTTPS slightly dropped. Sooner or later, HTTPS will become a standard consumers demand, and websites will need to have it in order to come across as trustworthy, reliable, and secure. 3. A secure website gives you a better reputation If visitors come to your website and can see your site information can be easily intercepted, it definitely does

docs.title: The Silent S in HTTPS
docs.text: The Silent S in HTTPS. not give a good impression. If your website is not safe, secure, and reliable, what makes you think your customers would risk purchasing from you when they can purchase similar products/services from your competitors with more secure websites? To ensure you maintain your company’s and brand’s good reputation, you should make a good first impression by showing that your site is HTTPS secured. HTTPS (Secure Hypertext Transport Protocol) HTTPS is a secure version of HTTP. This ensures that any communication sent online is secured by the SSL/TLS connection. Any ongoing communication between the server and browser will be encrypted for your safety. It allows you to evaluate how secure the environment is. If you are looking to establish an HTTPS connection, you will have to first purchase an SSL certificate from someone you can trust. You don’t want to purchase a certificate from just anyone. Look for trusted certificate authority. Then, you need to install it on the proper server. HTTPS is the code-text that is written using standard HTTPS format and secured with SSL/TLS to encrypt the HTTP text and ensure the communication is protected at all times. There are a number of reasons to use an HTTPS connection: - It helps to establish a secure communication between server and browser. - It secures websites against tampering activities or

docs.title: The Silent S in HTTPS
docs.text: The Silent S in HTTPS. eavesdropping. - It protects users from man-in-the-middle attacks. - It is used worldwide by business of all sizes to process secure payment transactions. - It is used by banking, healthcare, eCommerce, social media, and government industries. Regardless of what your situation might be, you need to look into the benefits of implementing SSL, HTTPS, and TLS secure connections in your business. You never know just how beneficial these secure methods are until you have to use them. In HTTPS, how does TLS/SSL encrypt HTTP requests and responses? TLS uses a technology called public key encryption: there are two keys, a public key and a private key, and the public key is shared with client devices via the server’s SSL certificate. When a client opens a connection with a server, the two devices use the public and private key to agree on new keys, called session keys, to encrypt further communications between them. All HTTP requests and responses are then encrypted with these session keys (this takes place at layer 6 in the OSI model), so that anyone who intercepts communications can only see a random string of characters, not the plaintext. ## But HTTPS doesn’t always mean the site is safe Let’s be honest, when most people see a little green lock with the word “Secure” to the left of

docs.title: The Silent S in HTTPS
docs.text: The Silent S in HTTPS. a URL, they think the site is safe. Ditto for spotting the words “this site uses a secure connection” or a URL beginning with the letters “https.” More and more sites these days are switching to HTTPS. Most have no choice, in fact. So what’s the problem? The more secure sites there are, the better — right? We’re about to let you in on a little secret: Those “Secure” symbols don’t guarantee a website is safe from all threats. A phishing site, for example, can legitimately display that comforting green lock next to its https address. So, what’s going on? Let’s find out. A secure connection does not mean a secure site The green lock means that the site has been issued a certificate and that a pair of cryptographic keys has been generated for it. Such sites encrypt information transmitted between you and the site. In this case, the page URLs begin with HTTPS, with the last “S” standing for “Secure.” Sure, encrypting transmitted data is a good thing. It means that information exchanged between your browser and the site is not accessible to third parties — ISPs, network administrators, intruders, and so on. It lets you enter passwords or credit card details without worrying about prying eyes. But the problem is that the green lock and the issued

docs.title: The Silent S in HTTPS
docs.text: The Silent S in HTTPS. certificate say nothing about the site itself. A phishing page can just as readily get a certificate and encrypt all traffic that flows between you and it. Put simply, all a green lock ensures is that no one _else_ can spy on the data you enter. But your password can still be stolen by the site itself, if it’s fake. Phishers make active use of this: According to Phishlabs, a quarter of all phishing attacks today are carried out on HTTPS sites (two years ago it was less than 1 percent). Moreover, more than 80 percent of users believe that the mere presence of a little green lock and the word “Secure” next to the URL means the site is safe, and they don’t think too hard before entering their data. How not to fall for the bait To sum up, the presence of a certificate and the green lock means only that the data transmitted between you and the site is encrypted, and that the certificate was issued by a trusted certificate authority. But it doesn’t prevent an HTTPS site from being malicious, a fact that is most skillfully manipulated by phishing scammers. So always be alert, no matter how safe the site seems at first glance. - Never enter logins, passwords, banking credentials, or any other personal information

docs.title: The Silent S in HTTPS
docs.text: The Silent S in HTTPS. on the site unless you are sure of its authenticity. To do so, always check the domain name — and very carefully; the name of a fake site might differ by only one character. And ensure links are reliable before clicking. - Always consider what a particular site is offering, whether it looks suspicious, and whether you really need to register on it. SSL (Secure Socket Layer) SSL was created by Netscape Communications Corporation back in 1994. It was designed to create a secure internet communication via the Web. It is a standard protocol that encrypts communication between your browser and the server, and allows for private information like social security numbers, credit card details, and login credentials to be transferred easily over the Internet. SSL utilizes two keys: - Public keys that are knowable by everyone. - Private keys known only by the person receiving the message. The two keys work together to form an encrypted connection via the Web. Being able to connect to a specific port requires a secure connection. As an example, you would use port 443 for HTTPS, 995 for secure POP3, 993 for secure IMAP, and so on. All of these ports are already set up on the server. They are ready to negotiate secure connections first, then they will proceed to do whatever

docs.title: The Silent S in HTTPS
docs.text: The Silent S in HTTPS. else you need after that. How does HTTPS help authenticate web servers? Authentication means verifying that a person or machine is who they claim to be. In HTTP, there is no verification of identity — it’s based on a principle of trust. The architects of HTTP didn’t necessarily make a decision to implicitly trust all web servers; they simply had priorities other than security at the time. But on the modern Internet, authentication is essential. Just like an ID card confirms a person’s identity, a private key confirms server identity. When a client opens a channel with an origin server (e.g. when a user navigates to a website), possession of the private key that matches with the public key in a website’s SSL certificate proves that the server is actually the legitimate host of the website. This prevents or helps block a number of attacks that are possible when there is no authentication, such as: - Man-in-the-middle attacks - DNS hijacking - BGP hijacking - Domain spoofing HTTPS myth-conceptions (src: CloudFlare) Many websites have been slow to adopt HTTPS. To explore why this is the case we have to look at the history. When HTTPS initially began rolling out, proper implementation was hard, slow, and expensive; it was hard to implement properly, slowed down Internet requests, and increased costs by

docs.title: The Silent S in HTTPS
docs.text: The Silent S in HTTPS. requiring expensive certificate services. None of these impediments remain true, but a lingering fear still exists for a lot of website owners, which has impeded some taking the leap into better security. Let’s explore some of the myths about HTTPS. “I don’t handle sensitive information on my website so I don’t need HTTPS” A common reason websites don’t implement security is because they think it’s overkill for their purposes. After all, if you’re not dealing with sensitive data, who cares if someone is snooping? There are a few reasons that this is an overly simplistic view on web security. For example, some Internet service providers will actually inject advertising into HTTP-served websites. These ads may or may not be in line with the content of the website, and can potentially be offensive, aside from the fact that the website provider has no creative input or share of the revenue. These injected ads are no longer feasible once a site is secured. Modern web browsers now limit functionality for sites that are not secure. Important features that improve the quality of the website now require HTTPS. Geolocation, push notifications and the service workers needed to run progressive web applications (PWAs) all require heightened security. This makes sense; data such as a user’s location is sensitive and can be used for nefarious

docs.title: The Silent S in HTTPS
docs.text: The Silent S in HTTPS. purposes. “I don’t want to damage my website’s performance by increasing my page load times” Performance is an important factor in both user experience and how Google returns results in search. Understandably, increasing latency is something to take seriously. Luckily, over time improvements have been made to HTTPS to reduce the performance overhead required to set up a encrypted connection. When an HTTP connection occurs, there are a number of trips the connection needs to make between the client requesting the webpage and the server. Aside from the normal latency associated with a TCP handshake (shown in blue below), an additional TLS/SSL handshake (shown in yellow) must occur to use HTTPS. _src: CloudFlare_ Improvements can be implemented to reduce the total latency of creating a SSL connection, including TLS session resumption and TLS false start. By using session resumption a server can keep a connection alive for longer by resuming the same session for additional requests. Keeping the connection alive saves time spent renegotiating the connection when the client requires an uncached origin fetch, reducing the total RTT by 50%. Another improvement to the speed at which an encrypted channel can be created is to implement a process called TLS false start, which cuts down on the latency by sending the encrypted data before the client has finished authentication. Last

docs.title: The Silent S in HTTPS
docs.text: The Silent S in HTTPS. but not least, HTTPS unlocks performance enhancements using HTTP/2 that let you do cool things like server pushing and multiplexing which can greatly optimize performance for HTTP requests. In total there is a significant performance benefit for making the switch. “It’s too expensive for me to implement HTTPS” At one point this may have been true, but now the cost is no longer a concern. “I’m going to lose search ranking while migrating my site to HTTPS” There are risks associated with website migration, and done improperly a negative SEO impact is possible. Potential pitfalls include website downtime, uncrawled webpages, and penalization for content duplication when two copies of the site exist at the same time. That said, websites can be migrated safely to HTTPS by following best practices. Two of the most important migration practices are: 1. using 301 redirects and 2) the proper placement of canonical tags. By using server 301 redirects on the HTTP site to point to the HTTPS version, a website tells Google to move to the new location for all search and indexing purposes. By placing canonical tags on the HTTPS site only, crawlers such as Googlebot will know that the new secure content should be considered canonical going forward. If you have a large number of pages and are concerned that the recrawl

docs.title: The Silent S in HTTPS
docs.text: The Silent S in HTTPS. will take too long, reach out to Google and tell them how much traffic you’re willing to put through your website. The network engineers will then crank up the crawl rate to help parse your site quickly and get it indexed. ## Stay Curious!

docs.title: What is Event Loop in JavaScript
docs.text: What is Event Loop in JavaScript. Introduction JavaScript Event Loop is one of the most fundamental concepts that every developer must aspire to understand. It is also one of the most frequently asked interview questions. JavaScript essentially is Single-threaded, i.e., it can only execute one task at a time. So, what happens if one request takes more than 2 minutes to execute? Will the user be kept waiting for ever? It certainly not an ideal situation. Thankfully, JavaScript’s Event loop architecture comes to the rescue, as it provides the ability to process multiple requests asynchronously. We will first look at the following components that constitute Event Loop Architecture. The Call Stack Web API Event Queue Once we try and understand how they work together, then explaining Event Loop becomes very simple. Call Stack The Call Stack is a part of the JavaScript Engine and it is simply a stack in which you can add an item and the item added first is processed last. In other words, it follows the FILO - ‘First In Last Out’ principle. A Call Stack acts as a placeholder or a holding area for all the JavaScript functions that have been fired for execution. Let us look at the below code sample and understand how the function ‘sayHello’ gets added to the Call Stack. Step 1 - sayHello Function gets added

docs.text: What is Event Loop in JavaScript. to the Call Stack From the illustration below, you can see once the function sayHello() is invoked, it is added to the call stack. Step 2 & 3 - Function returns a value & gets popped from the Call Stack Once the function returns a value, the output ‘Hello from Skay’ gets displayed on the console. As soon as the function returns, almost immediately, the function is also popped off from the call stack. Now, let’s look at the below code example, with two functions and understand how the JavaScript Engine executes it. As discussed previously, the two functions are added to the Call Stack as shown below. And the function sayHello() is popped off the stack once the function execution completes. However, as for the second function ‘timeoutFunction’, it returns a setTimeout function which is a part of the Web API. Let us look at what Web API is first. Web API Web APIs are built into your web browser and they are able to process data from the browser to do complex useful things. The main thing to understand is that, they are not a part of the JavaScript language, but, they are built on top of the core JS language and provide much more capabilities such as Geolocation, localstorage, etc. So, coming back to our code example,

docs.title: What is Event Loop in JavaScript
docs.text: What is Event Loop in JavaScript. when the function ‘timeoutFunction’ is executed, it returns the ‘setTimeout’ function and is popped off the stack. Since the ‘setTimeout’ function is part of the Web API, it gets moved to the Web API as shown below. Along with that, the timer function in Web API is set to 1 second (1000 ms) based on the argument we had passed to the ‘setTimeout’ function as shown in the illustration below. So, what happens after one second? Ideally, you would have anticipated that the function is returned back to the Call Stack for execution. However, instead, it adds it to the Event Queue. Event Queue Event Queue is a data structure similar to Stack, which holds the data temporarily and the important thing to note is that the data added first is processed first. In other words, it follows the FIFO -> ‘First in First out’ principle. So after one second, the ‘setTimeout’ function from Web API is added to the Queue as shown below. Event Loop Finally, the ‘Event Loop’ we’ve been waiting for. The function of Event Loop can simply be explained as connecting the Event Queue to the Call Stack. Event Loop does the following: Checks if the Call Stack is empty, i.e., if all the functions have completed their execution and they have been popped off the

docs.title: What is Event Loop in JavaScript
docs.text: What is Event Loop in JavaScript. Call Stack. Once the Call Stack is empty, it moves the first item from the Event Queue to the Call Stack. When the setTimeout function gets added to the Call Stack, the function simply returns the output ‘Hello from Timeout Function’ on the console and is popped out of the Stack. That’s all there is to know about Event Loop. Hope the explanation with illustrations provided a way to understand Event Loop in a simple manner. In fact, there’s a tool to visualize the Even Loop in real time built by Philip Roberts, which you can access from this link. Conclusion To summarize, in this article, we learnt about how JavaScript is Single-Threaded in nature and using Event Loop, it supports processing multiple-requests with the help of a Call Stack, Web API and Event Queue. Event Loop is basically the way where JavaScript engine looks at the queue to find out if there are any immediate functions to run and picks the one added first and moves it to the Call Stack. We demonstrated the above concept using the asynchronous setTimeout function which is a part of the Web API. Fin!

docs.title: An AI Agent Sandbox Is Not Your Authorization Boundary
docs.text: An AI Agent Sandbox Is Not Your Authorization Boundary. Your agent needs to inspect a repository, run tests, and suggest a patch. It does not need permission to merge a PR. Those two requirements are easy to blur when a managed agent comes with its own sandbox. OpenAI's Agents API launched in public beta on September 10, 2026. It supplies the agent harness and lets developers choose an OpenAI-hosted environment or their own infrastructure. The quickstart creates a session in an openai_hosted environment and streams progress. This removes a lot of orchestration work. It does not transfer your application's authorization policy into the sandbox. A sandbox limits where code runs. Your application decides what the agent may change. This is a design recommendation, not a claim that a particular sandbox has been breached. Five separate questions hiding behind “is it sandboxed?” | Boundary | Question to answer before launch | Default for a patch-review agent | | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | | Execution | Where can generated code run? | Disposable, task-scoped workspace | | Network | Which destinations can it reach? | No outbound access unless the task needs it | | Credentials | What secret material can agent-generated code read? | No production credentials in the workspace | | Authorization | Who decides whether a proposed action is permitted? | Application-side policy, not agent prose

docs.title: An AI Agent Sandbox Is Not Your Authorization Boundary
docs.text: An AI Agent Sandbox Is Not Your Authorization Boundary. | | Durable state | Who applies changes to the real repository or deployment? | Human-reviewed PR; no merge or deploy permission | The first two rows are environment configuration. The last two are product behavior. Don't treat a green check on the first row as an answer to all five. OpenAI's hosted-sandbox documentation says outbound network access is enabled by default unless a template policy changes it. It offers disabled and restricted modes; restricted mode uses exact hostnames rather than wildcard domains. The same documentation says ordinary env variables are readable by agent-generated code and directs developers to use vault credentials for secrets instead. These are useful controls, but you must choose them explicitly for your workload. A domain allowlist controls a destination, not which operation the agent may perform at that destination. Try the design review before reading mine Scenario: A coding agent checks a dependency upgrade in an unfamiliar repository. It needs package installation, tests, and a patch for review. Pick the smallest permission set you would grant. Decision A: does an isolated workspace make generated code trustworthy? A sandbox limits the process environment; it doesn't establish that the patch is correct or safe. Keep each run disposable and task-scoped, then review the returned diff and rerun checks in a trusted CI environment against the exact revision.

docs.title: An AI Agent Sandbox Is Not Your Authorization Boundary
docs.text: An AI Agent Sandbox Is Not Your Authorization Boundary. Decision B: allow outbound internet for package installation? First ask whether a prebuilt dependency cache or a setup step can satisfy the task. If the agent must fetch packages, restrict destinations as tightly as the build allows and pin dependency versions; don't assume an allowlisted package host makes package contents trustworthy. The hosted-sandbox docs warn that redirects and subdomains need separate allowlist entries. Re-run the install in a clean workspace before trusting the result. Decision C: put a GitHub token in the sandbox so it can open a PR? Keep a repo-scoped write token out of agent-generated code. Let the agent return a patch or artifact, validate it outside the workspace, and let a separate application service open the PR with the smallest necessary credential. OpenAI documents /workspace/outputs as the location for published, immutable artifacts when a turn completes; an artifact is output to inspect, not an authorization grant. If your workflow genuinely needs agent-accessible credentials, review the provider's vault-credential mechanism and its scope instead of putting a secret in env . Decision D: should the agent decide which actions are authorized? No. Treat model output, generated code, and tool requests as untrusted proposals. Enforce authorization in application-side policy at every tool boundary; the agent's explanation, a successful run, or a hostname allowlist is not that policy. Decision E: should

docs.title: An AI Agent Sandbox Is Not Your Authorization Boundary
docs.text: An AI Agent Sandbox Is Not Your Authorization Boundary. a passing test run let the agent merge or deploy? No. An agent's summary is not a test attestation. Run the repository's checks in a separate trusted CI context against the exact proposed commit; review the diff and source of any downloaded dependencies. A merge is a different capability from preparing a patch. Make the human or a separately specified deployment policy authorize it. These aren't model-quality questions. They are questions about where untrusted inputs become durable effects. A narrow handoff you can implement A safe first version of this workflow has three stages: 1. Run: give the agent a repository snapshot and a task, with no production secrets. Set an explicit network policy. Record the input revision and environment configuration alongside the run. 2. Inspect: collect its patch, explanation, and command output. Treat all three as untrusted. Check that the diff touches only allowed paths; run format, type, and test checks yourself against the exact patch. A passing check means _those checks_ passed, not that the change is secure. 3. Propose: a separate service, holding a scoped GitHub credential, opens a review-only PR. Require another authorization step for merge or deploy. Never use the agent's self-reported success as the condition for production writes. The last two stages are an application-side architecture proposal, not features automatically supplied by the Agents

docs.text: An AI Agent Sandbox Is Not Your Authorization Boundary. API. OpenAI's quickstart also says to keep the application API key outside the sandbox and lists separate permissions for agent sessions and model inference. That is a helpful reminder: even the API used to _start_ a run has a different trust boundary from the code running _inside_ one. There is a tradeoff. A no-network environment cannot install new dependencies from a registry; a review-only agent cannot autonomously ship a fix. Start there if the job is “prepare a patch.” Widen one capability at a time, with a concrete task that needs it and a check you can run independently. “It ran in a sandbox” is the beginning of that review, not the end. For a runnable companion, see testing AI agent actions with an approval gate. docs.title: AGENTS.md Is Becoming the Most Important File in Your Repository
docs.text: AGENTS.md Is Becoming the Most Important File in Your Repository. The most consequential file in your repository may no longer be package.json , Dockerfile , or README.md . It is increasingly the small Markdown file that tells an AI agent what all of those files _mean_. Call it AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md , or .github/copilot-instructions.md ; the filename is less important than the shift behind it. Coding agents are moving from autocomplete into repositories, terminals, pull requests, and CI. In that world, the quality of the work is no longer determined only by the model you picked. It is determined by whether the repository can explain itself before the agent starts changing it. This is not a niche workflow for people who enjoy configuring tools. GitHub's current documentation says its cloud agent and CLI can load AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md , and GEMINI.md , alongside repository- and path-specific instructions. OpenAI's Codex agent loop also loads AGENTS.md ; Anthropic's Claude Code has the equivalent CLAUDE.md project memory. The tools are competing. The pattern is converging. That is why a good instruction file is becoming engineering infrastructure—not a prompt. The data says the work is already changing Anthropic's June 2026 study of roughly 400,000 Claude Code sessions found that people still make most of the planning decisions—what to build—while the agent makes most execution decisions—how to build it. Over the study period, the share

docs.title: AGENTS.md Is Becoming the Most Important File in Your Repository
docs.text: AGENTS.md Is Becoming the Most Important File in Your Repository. of sessions spent debugging fell by almost half, and the estimated value of the typical task rose about 25% . The important finding is the one that gets lost in the "AI replaces developers" argument: people with more domain knowledge got more useful work out of the agent. The machine did not make context irrelevant. It made context more valuable. Your repository is where that context lives: - why the payment flow is deliberately awkward; - which API response is a public contract, not an implementation detail; - where auth, telemetry, and rate limiting are handled; - which command proves a change works; and - which "obvious cleanup" would quietly break production. An agent can infer some of this by reading files. It cannot reliably infer all of it, and making it rediscover the same rules on every task is a strange way to spend a context window. Your repo is now part of the prompt For years, teams treated repository documentation as a thing written for the next human developer. Agent instructions change the audience, not the underlying job. You are still preserving decisions, naming the hazards, and making the safe path obvious. The difference is that the reader can now edit 40 files and run commands before you have made a coffee. This is the same reason good runbooks beat company values at 2 a.m. Specificity is not bureaucracy. It is a shortcut to a correct decision. The instruction file should be a map, not a constitution The common failure mode is taking every tribal rule in a company and pasting it into one enormous Markdown file. That creates a new problem: the agent pays attention to the generic rules and misses the one detail that

It recommends repository-wide instructions for durable conventions, but says that instructions which are too large or too specific can distract from the immediate task; use a skill or a custom agent for focused workflows instead. Think in three layers: Your root AGENTS.md should cover the first layer. Keep it short enough that a human can audit it in one sitting. Put database rules near database code. Put your release checklist in a release playbook. The exact support varies by tool, but the design principle does not: give the agent the smallest useful context at the point where it needs it. What belongs in a good AGENTS.md Here is the skeleton I would start with for a web application: That is deliberately boring. It contains no model-specific magic words and no inspirational advice. It tells a capable agent where it is, how the codebase is shaped, how to prove a change, and what it must not casually damage. The exact details should come from the repository, not a template. If your app uses pnpm , do not copy the Bun command. If deployment has a migration gate, name it. If the fastest local test is a single Playwright project, make that the default. A lie

docs.text: AGENTS.md Is Becoming the Most Important File in Your Repository. in an agent instruction file is worse than no instruction file because it causes a confident wrong action. Write rules that survive a model change The model race is moving too quickly to write your process around one vendor's quirks. A durable instruction describes the desired engineering outcome and the available evidence, not a chain of prompts optimized for this month's agent. Good: Fragile: The first tells any agent—and any human reviewer—what success looks like. The second asks for an internal state you cannot inspect or verify. The same rule applies to tool permissions. Describe allowed operations and their boundaries. "Do not delete production data" is vague. "Production database commands are read-only unless a human has approved the exact migration" is an operational control. Agents are powerful precisely because they can use tools; instructions should reduce blast radius, not merely ask the model to be cautious. For a deeper look at those security boundaries, see my guide to AI agents, MCP, and the next supply-chain risk. Instructions are not a substitute for tests This distinction matters more as the files get better. AGENTS.md is a steering layer. Tests, types, linters, CI checks, permissions, and code review are the enforcement layer. An instruction can tell an agent to preserve a response shape. A contract test is what catches the accidental change.

docs.text: AGENTS.md Is Becoming the Most Important File in Your Repository. An instruction can tell an agent not to weaken authorization. A permission boundary and a regression test are what make the rule credible. That is also why agents reward well-maintained projects unevenly. A repository with fast tests, crisp boundaries, and useful docs gives an agent short feedback loops. A repository with no checks gives it a large space in which to be confidently wrong. The practical loop is simple: If an agent repeatedly misses the same rule, do not immediately add another paragraph of admonitions. First ask which layer failed: - Was the rule absent or hard to find? Improve the relevant instruction. - Was the rule clear but not testable? Add a guardrail or regression test. - Was the task too broad? Break it into a smaller handoff. - Was the agent allowed to touch too much? Narrow permissions or isolate the environment. That diagnosis produces a system improvement. A larger prompt usually produces only a larger prompt. Treat the file like production code The best way to maintain agent instructions is to edit them when reality changes, not during an annual documentation drive. Add a line when a production incident reveals a non-obvious invariant. Remove a line when the rule is duplicated elsewhere or no longer true. Review instruction changes in pull requests with the same skepticism you

Three useful questions for every addition: 1. Would a new human engineer make a worse decision without this? If not, it probably does not belong in shared instructions. 2. Can I make this rule observable? Prefer a command, path, test, or interface over an adjective. 3. Is this global, local, or task-specific? Put it in the narrowest place that will still be discovered. The syntax is not the point. Whether your team standardizes on AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md , or a vendor-specific instruction path, the useful content is remarkably portable. That portability is the opportunity: write down the engineering knowledge that should outlive a tool choice. The real moat is legible engineering Coding agents will keep getting cheaper, faster, and more autonomous. GitHub has already added model selection, self-review, security scanning, custom agents, and CLI handoff to its coding agent. The agent itself is becoming a commodity feature. The durable advantage is a codebase that can be safely understood by a new contributor—human or artificial—without oral history, detective work, or a week of Slack archaeology. AGENTS.md will not make a bad architecture good. It will not replace a test suite. It will not turn a vague product request into a correct implementation. But it gives every future agent

docs.title: AI Agents Didn't Kill Junior Developer Jobs. They Killed the Reason to Hire Them.
docs.text: AI Agents Didn't Kill Junior Developer Jobs. They Killed the Reason to Hire Them.. Here's a contradiction nobody in tech wants to say out loud: 92% of companies plan to hire this year , and entry-level engineering postings have collapsed 20-35% globally over the same stretch. Google and Meta are hiring roughly half as many new grads as they did in 2021. At Big Tech overall, new grads now make up about 7% of hires , down from 32% in 2019 . Both of those things are true at once. That's not a hiring freeze. It's a hiring _rewrite_ — and if you're a junior developer, or you manage a team of them, you need to understand exactly what got rewritten, because "learn to code" was never the part that was fragile. The jobs didn't disappear. The task list did. The honest mechanical reason is unglamorous: there is no economic incentive to hire a junior engineer who takes three days to do what an agent finishes in three minutes. Boilerplate, CRUD scaffolding, simple bug fixes, first-draft docs, "implement this well-specified ticket" — that entire category of work is exactly what coding agents are good at today, and it also happens to be exactly the category of work junior engineers used to cut their teeth on. It wasn't busywork. It was the training pipeline. And it just got automated out from under the people who

docs.title: AI Agents Didn't Kill Junior Developer Jobs. They Killed the Reason to Hire Them.
docs.text: AI Agents Didn't Kill Junior Developer Jobs. They Killed the Reason to Hire Them.. needed it. Meanwhile the postings that _are_ growing tell the other half of the story. AI/ML engineering now leads every hiring category, up 163% year over year , with 500,000+ open roles globally and roughly 3.4 open AI roles per qualified candidate . AI skill requirements now show up in 73% of U.S. tech job postings , up from 71% the month before, and up 192% year-over-year . Demand for engineers didn't fall. Demand for a specific, cheap kind of engineering labor did. Nobody's hiring "coders" anymore. They're hiring supervisors. Fortune profiled this shift back in March as the rise of what they called "the supervisor class" — engineers whose primary value is no longer writing the code, but orchestrating the agents that write it, reviewing what comes out, and making the architectural calls that decide whether the whole system holds together. That's not a euphemism for "manager." It's a genuinely different skill: - Context design — structuring a codebase, its docs, and its interfaces so an agent can actually operate inside it without hallucinating half the API surface. - Agent orchestration — defining roles, tool access, and hand-off rules when multiple agents are working a task in parallel, which is now commanding premium comp precisely because almost nobody can do it well yet. - Validation judgment — knowing _when_

AI output is right, when it's confidently wrong, and being able to explain the difference to a security reviewer or a product owner. Hiring managers have quietly updated the interview script to match. The question isn't "have you used Copilot or Cursor" anymore — everyone has. It's "when do you choose _not_ to use it, and how do you verify what it gave you." Engineers who can answer that with a real story are being hired over engineers who can't, at every level, junior included. So what do you actually do with this? If you're early-career, the uncomfortable truth is that the old apprenticeship path — get hired, get assigned small well-defined tickets, build judgment slowly — is narrower than it was three years ago. The counter isn't to avoid AI tools; it's the opposite. Show up already fluent, and spend your visible effort on the 20% of the job an agent still can't do for you: reading a vague requirement and turning it into a real spec, catching the security implication nobody wrote down, deciding whether the fast path is the right path. That's the part hiring managers are explicitly screening for right now, and it's learnable faster than "years of experience" implies. If you're senior or hiring, the leverage move is the same one that always wins in

The engineers commanding the new premium aren't the ones who adopted the tools fastest — they're the ones who can tell you, with specifics, where the tools stop being trustworthy. The market isn't shrinking. It's re-pricing a skill that used to be scarce — writing code — now that it's cheap, and re-pricing a skill that used to be implicit — judgment about code — now that it's the whole job. --- Sources: The Pragmatic Engineer — State of the Software Engineering Job Market 2026, Dice Tech Job Report, June 2026, The New Stack — "AI is disrupting everything": Where do entry-level tech jobs go now?, IEEE Spectrum — How to Stay Ahead of AI as an Early-Career Engineer, KORE1 — Agentic AI Engineering Hiring Survey 2026, Fortune's March 2026 profile on engineering's "supervisor class."

docs.title: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk
docs.text: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk. The thing I underestimated about AI coding tools is not how fast they can write code. It is how quickly they are becoming part of the execution path. For the last few years, most developers treated AI assistants like smarter autocomplete. The assistant suggested a function, explained an error, generated a test, or helped refactor a component. That workflow had risk, but the boundary was still clear: the AI produced text, and the developer decided what to run. That boundary is changing. AI agents can now read repositories, inspect issues, call tools, run tests, modify files, open pull requests, and connect to external systems through protocols like MCP. Once an AI system can use tools, the security question changes completely. The risk is no longer only: "Did the model generate incorrect code?" The risk becomes: "What is this agent allowed to do, what can influence it, and where can data flow after it acts?" That is the lesson I took away from looking at the current AI agent ecosystem: AI coding is becoming a software supply chain problem. Why This Changed My Mental Model Stack Overflow's 2025 Developer Survey shows the contradiction developers are living with. AI tool adoption reached 80%, but trust in AI accuracy dropped to 29%. The survey also found that 66% of developers spend more time

docs.title: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk
docs.text: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk. fixing "almost-right" AI-generated code, and 52% say AI agents have already changed how they complete work. That combination matters. Developers are using AI more, trusting it less, and still moving toward workflows where AI has more agency. That is a strange place to be. It means the tools are useful enough to become normal, but unreliable enough that we need stronger engineering discipline around them. The mistake is thinking the main issue is hallucination. Hallucination is annoying. A tool-connected agent with excessive permissions is dangerous. Bad code can fail tests. A badly constrained agent can read secrets, call APIs, mutate infrastructure, publish data, or create a pull request that changes how CI behaves. That is a different class of problem. What MCP Actually Is MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a standard way for AI applications to connect to tools and data sources. The simple explanation is: MCP lets AI agents use external capabilities without every AI app needing a custom integration for every tool. An MCP server can expose: - tools, such as reading files, querying a database, creating GitHub issues, running kubectl , or searching internal docs; - resources, such as tickets, logs, source files, metrics, design docs, or API references; - prompts and templates that guide how the model should use those capabilities. Anthropic donated MCP to

docs.title: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk
docs.text: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk. the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025. At that point, Anthropic said MCP had crossed 10,000 active public servers and had been adopted across products including ChatGPT, Cursor, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Visual Studio Code, and other AI tools. That adoption tells us something important: MCP is not a niche plugin format anymore. It is becoming a common integration layer for agentic software. And every integration layer eventually becomes a security boundary. The Old Supply Chain vs. The Agent Supply Chain Developers already understand traditional software supply chain risk. We worry about: - npm packages; - Docker images; - GitHub Actions; - CI runners; - package lockfiles; - base images; - transitive dependencies; - build scripts; - deployment credentials. AI agents add a new layer on top of that. Now we also need to worry about: - tool descriptions that the model treats as instructions; - MCP servers installed from public repositories; - OAuth grants attached to AI clients; - local tools with access to the developer machine; - agent memory that mixes trusted and untrusted text; - prompts embedded inside tickets, docs, comments, or files; - tool responses that can influence later tool calls; - automated pull requests that modify executable project configuration. This is the key shift: If an agent can call a tool, that tool is

docs.title: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk
docs.text: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk. part of your software supply chain. It does not matter if the UI looks like chat. Underneath the UI, you may be giving a probabilistic planner access to files, credentials, network calls, source control, and production-shaped systems. That is powerful. It is also exactly the kind of thing engineers should threat-model. What Made Me Take MCP Security Seriously The security research around MCP is still young, but the pattern is already clear. OWASP now has an MCP Security Cheat Sheet. OWASP also documents MCP tool poisoning as a specific attack pattern. OX Security published MCP research in April 2026 claiming a broad supply-chain issue affecting 150M+ downloads and up to 200,000 vulnerable instances. On May 12, 2026, OX followed with additional MCP-related findings in tools such as kubectl-mcp-server, Archon OS, and MarkItDown. Security vendor research should always be read with healthy skepticism. Headlines can overstate. Numbers can depend on assumptions. But the underlying concern is real: AI agents are connecting to tools faster than teams are defining permissions, audit trails, sandboxing, and review practices. That is how normal developer convenience turns into infrastructure risk. Attack Pattern 1: Tool Poisoning Tool poisoning is what changed my view of agent security the most. A normal application calls an API and receives data. An AI agent calls a tool and receives data that

docs.title: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk
docs.text: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk. may become part of its reasoning context. That difference matters. If a malicious or compromised MCP server can influence the model through tool descriptions, schemas, or responses, the server may not need direct access to the most sensitive system. It can try to persuade the agent to use another tool that has stronger permissions. For example: 1. A documentation tool returns a normal-looking answer with hidden or indirect instructions. 2. The agent treats the tool response as useful context. 3. The agent then calls a GitHub, filesystem, shell, Slack, or database tool. 4. Sensitive data leaves through a tool call that looks legitimate in isolation. This is why prompt injection becomes more serious in agentic systems. The injected text is not just trying to change an answer. It may be trying to change a sequence of actions. That is the part developers need to internalize. Prompt injection against a chatbot is a content integrity issue. Prompt injection against a tool-using agent can become an authorization issue. Attack Pattern 2: The Confused Deputy The confused deputy problem is old, but agents make it easy to recreate. Imagine a user asks an agent to summarize an internal document. The agent uses an MCP server that has broad access to many systems. The user may not have permission to read everything the MCP

docs.title: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk
docs.text: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk. server can read, but the tool acts with its own credentials. Now the agent is not acting with the user's authority. It is acting with the tool's authority. That is dangerous because the user interface hides the privilege boundary. The developer sees: "Summarize this." The system may actually perform: "Use a broadly scoped service token to search internal docs, tickets, repositories, and messages, then decide what context is relevant." If the server does not enforce user-scoped authorization, the agent can become a path around the permission model. The fix is not glamorous: least privilege, user-scoped auth where possible, short-lived tokens, and separate credentials per tool. Boring security controls become very interesting when the thing using the credential is non-deterministic. Attack Pattern 3: Local Tool Access Local MCP servers are useful because they can connect an agent to the developer's real environment. They can read files. They can run commands. They can inspect logs. They can talk to local services. They can sometimes see configuration that was never meant to leave the machine. That is also why they need more caution. A developer laptop often contains: - SSH keys; - cloud credentials; - .env files; - package registry tokens; - local databases; - browser session state; - private notes; - customer or production debugging data; - cloned repositories from multiple projects.

docs.title: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk
docs.text: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk. If an MCP server can access the whole machine, the agent's effective context is much larger than the current repository. One bad tool, one bad prompt injection, or one over-broad file read can cross boundaries the developer did not intend to connect. The practical lesson is simple: Run agent tools inside the smallest environment that can do the job. For coding work, that usually means the repository and its test environment. It should not mean the entire home directory, personal documents, browser profile, SSH folder, and every cloned project. Attack Pattern 4: Pull Requests as Execution Vehicles At first, agent-created pull requests feel safer than direct commits. And they are safer, because they create a review point. But a pull request is not just text. A pull request can change: - package scripts; - CI workflows; - Dockerfiles; - dependency versions; - lockfiles; - code generation steps; - test commands; - build configuration; - deployment scripts; - GitHub Actions permissions. That means agent-created diffs need a different review habit. It is not enough to skim the application code and see whether the feature works. You also have to inspect the executable parts of the change. A one-line modification in .github/workflows/deploy.yml may matter more than 300 lines of harmless UI code. GitHub's Copilot cloud agent documentation describes guardrails such as isolated

docs.title: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk
docs.text: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk. branches and workflow approval controls. Those guardrails are useful, but they do not remove the need for human review. They just give the review a better shape. The safest default is: - agents can propose; - humans review; - protected branches enforce policy; - workflow changes require extra attention; - deployment remains explicitly approved. The Mistake I See Coming The mistake I expect many teams to make is treating agents like productivity tools while configuring them like infrastructure. The interface says chat. The permissions say automation worker. The actual system may behave like: - a CI runner; - a shell script; - a browser automation tool; - a GitHub bot; - an API gateway; - a package installer; - a junior developer with credentials. That mismatch is where incidents happen. If an AI agent can call tools, read files, and write code, it should be managed like a privileged development process. Not like a browser tab you happen to type into. The Security Model I Would Use The most useful mental model I found is this: An AI agent is a process with a probabilistic planner and a tool belt. Secure the process, the tool belt, and the data paths between them. That gives us three questions. First: what can the agent observe? Can it read the whole repository? Can

docs.title: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk
docs.text: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk. it read .env files? Can it inspect private docs? Can it see customer data? Can it read tickets that contain credentials or internal URLs? Second: what can the agent do? Can it write files? Run shell commands? Install packages? Open pull requests? Send Slack messages? Query production? Deploy? Delete resources? Third: what can influence the agent? Can issue comments, docs, README files, logs, web pages, dependency output, or tool responses change what it does next? That third question is easy to forget. In normal software, untrusted input might break a parser or alter a query. In agentic software, untrusted input can alter the plan. My Practical Checklist If I were adding AI agents and MCP tools to a development workflow, I would start with this checklist. 1. Inventory Every Tool List every AI client, every MCP server, every connector, and every credential. For each one, write down: - what it can read; - what it can write; - whether it can execute commands; - whether it can access the network; - which credentials it receives; - who approved it; - how it is updated; - how it is removed. If the team cannot answer these questions, the team does not understand its agent surface area yet. 2. Use Narrow Credentials Do not give a general agent a general token. Prefer:

docs.title: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk
docs.text: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk. - repo-scoped GitHub credentials; - read-only tokens by default; - separate tokens per MCP server; - short-lived credentials; - user-scoped authorization where possible; - no production secrets in local agent contexts; - no shared automation super-token. This is the same least-privilege idea we already know. Agents just make the cost of ignoring it higher. 3. Sandbox Local Servers Local MCP servers should not automatically inherit the whole laptop. Use containers, project-specific working directories, read-only mounts, and explicit network rules where possible. At minimum, avoid giving local agent tools access to: - ~/.ssh ; - cloud credential folders; - password manager exports; - browser profiles; - unrelated repositories; - real production .env files. The goal is not perfect isolation. The goal is to make the common failure modes boring. 4. Separate Read, Write, and Release Do not put every capability into one agent context. Use separate modes: - research mode can read but not write; - implementation mode can edit files in a branch; - review mode can inspect diffs and logs; - release mode requires explicit approval. This adds friction, but it also makes behavior understandable. A single all-powerful agent is convenient until you need to explain an incident. 5. Make Tool Calls Visible Approvals should show the real operation. Weak approval: "Allow agent to update project?" Useful approval: "Allow

docs.text: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk. github.createPullRequest in piyush97/PiyushMehta.com from branch blog/ai-angents-mcp-post with these changed files?" For sensitive actions, show: - tool name; - target system; - parameters; - data leaving the machine; - files being changed; - command being executed. Humans cannot approve what they cannot see. 6. Review Tool Definitions Like Code Tool names, descriptions, schemas, and prompts shape model behavior. That means they should be reviewed. Pin versions. Diff updates. Avoid vague tools that accept arbitrary commands. Prefer small tools with clear parameters. Watch for tool description changes that alter how the agent is instructed to behave. This feels strange only because the industry is still learning that prompts and tool schemas are executable influence. 7. Log Enough To Debug Incidents A final pull request is not a full audit trail. For important work, keep records of: - tool calls; - commands run; - files read; - URLs contacted; - credentials requested; - credentials denied; - tests executed; - approval events; - final diffs. If something goes wrong, you need to know whether the problem came from the prompt, the model, the tool, the environment, or the permission model. Without logs, every agent incident becomes a guessing game. The Individual Developer Version If you are using AI coding agents by yourself, the practical version is: - keep agents inside the project directory; -

docs.title: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk
docs.text: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk. do not expose real production .env files; - review shell commands before running them; - inspect workflow, package, Docker, and lockfile changes carefully; - use read-only connectors until write access is clearly needed; - revoke tokens for tools you stop using; - avoid installing random MCP servers into your main development environment; - assume anything the agent can read may influence what it does next. The agent can move fast. Your job is to decide where it is allowed to move. The Team Version For teams, this becomes policy: - maintain an approved MCP/tool registry; - require review for new agent tools; - manage per-tool credentials centrally; - restrict network egress from agent sandboxes; - protect branches from direct agent writes; - require extra review for CI and deployment changes; - scan agent branches for secrets; - log agent sessions; - define who owns agent-authored changes after merge. The ownership part matters. If an agent opens a PR and a human merges it, the team owns the result. The model does not carry the pager. What I Believe Now I do not think AI agents should be banned from development workflows. I think they should be treated honestly. They are not just autocomplete. They are not just chat. They are becoming tool-using development processes that sit inside the same systems

docs.title: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk
docs.text: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk. we use to build, test, review, and ship software. That makes them useful. It also makes them part of the supply chain. The teams that handle this well will not be the teams that connect every possible tool to every possible model. They will be the teams that make agent work observable, scoped, reversible, and reviewable. That is the real lesson for me: AI agents are not dangerous because they are intelligent. They are dangerous when they are connected to powerful tools without clear boundaries. Boundaries are the product work now. docs.title: Is AI Rotting Your Brain? The Attention and Critical Thinking Trap
docs.text: Is AI Rotting Your Brain? The Attention and Critical Thinking Trap. You ask AI to summarize an article. Then to explain the summary. Then to write your response. Twenty minutes later, you have a polished opinion you cannot defend without reopening the chat. That is the real AI brain-rot question: are you saving time on a task, or skipping the thinking the task was supposed to teach you? “Brain rot” is a catchy phrase, not a medical diagnosis. The evidence does not show that using ChatGPT permanently damages your brain or gives everyone an eight-second attention span. It does show a more specific risk: when a tool repeatedly does the reading, recalling, and evaluating for you, you may engage less with those parts of the work. Meanwhile, fast answers and endless AI-generated content make it easier to leave a hard question before you have wrestled with it. The evidence, without the scary headline Three studies often get blended into one claim. They measured different things. The CHI 2025 study is especially relevant to office work. Its 319 participants supplied 936 first-hand examples. Higher confidence in the AI's answer was associated with less self-reported critical thinking ; higher confidence in their own ability was associated with more. The authors also found that thinking did not simply disappear: it shifted toward verifying information, integrating responses, and supervising the task. This was a survey,

docs.title: Is AI Rotting Your Brain? The Attention and Critical Thinking Trap
docs.text: Is AI Rotting Your Brain? The Attention and Critical Thinking Trap. so it cannot establish that AI _caused_ a decline. The MIT Media Lab essay study assigned participants to write with ChatGPT, search, or no tool. Across three sessions, the LLM group showed the weakest EEG connectivity and reported the least ownership of its essays. Many struggled to quote what they had written. In a fourth session, a smaller group switched tools, and prior LLM users still showed lower engagement on some measures when writing unaided. This is a provocative small preprint about essay writing , not a diagnosis of atrophy. EEG connectivity is a measure of activity during a task; it is not a measure of someone's intelligence. And the viral “LLMs Can Get Brain Rot” paper is about models , not people. Its revised version reports that four models continually trained on more low-quality social-media text performed worse on some reasoning and long-context benchmarks. WIRED's coverage describes the earlier experiment. A model trained on junk text is an important data-quality story; it is not an experiment showing that scrolling changes a human brain in the same way. Does AI actually shorten your attention span? We do not have good evidence that ChatGPT use, by itself, permanently reduces a person's general attention span. “Attention span” also is not one fixed number. Staying with a difficult proof, resisting a notification, and

docs.title: Is AI Rotting Your Brain? The Attention and Critical Thinking Trap
docs.text: Is AI Rotting Your Brain? The Attention and Critical Thinking Trap. recalling a paragraph are different tasks. The more defensible concern is fragmented attention during work . A hard question becomes a prompt. The answer produces five possible follow-up prompts. A notification arrives. You switch from the original problem to evaluating an output, then to chasing another one. Research on interrupted work found that interruptions can raise stress even when people compensate by working faster. That study predates modern chatbots; it supports the cost of interruption, not a claim that AI has rewired your attention. AI can also make the switch away from difficulty unusually attractive. A polished answer arrives before you have formed a hypothesis. If you always choose the easy exit, you get less practice holding a question in mind. That is a plausible habit mechanism , not a proven, permanent change in brain capacity. There is a second route: AI makes new posts, summaries, and clips cheap to produce, so a feed can offer more chances to switch away from a demanding task. WIRED notes the concern that AI-generated slop can feed the next generation of models, too. The possible human attention cost comes from the feed and the habit of switching , not from the model-training experiment itself. AI can remove precisely those steps: 1. You skip retrieval. Instead of trying to remember or reconstruct an idea, you ask for it. docs.text: How I Designed an AI Chat App That Handles a Million Users (And the Mistakes That Almost Killed It). I was six months into building what I thought was a straightforward AI chat app when a single user sent me a message that changed everything. _"Your app is great but it takes 12 seconds to respond. My ChatGPT answers in 2. I'm switching back."_ That was the moment I realized: building an AI chat that works for 10 users and building one that works for a million are two completely different engineering problems. The first is a weekend project. The second nearly broke me. Here's what I learned — the architecture, the trade-offs, the fires I put out, and the three production incidents that taught me more than any system design book ever did. The Naive Architecture (What I Built First) Let me be honest about what I shipped to production the first time, because I know someone reading this has done the same thing. Version 1.0: - Node.js server with a single WebSocket connection - Direct OpenAI API calls from the server - In-memory message storage - One process, one queue, prayers It worked perfectly for me and my 15 beta testers. Then we hit 500 concurrent users and the server fell over like a Jenga tower at a toddler's birthday party. The Wake-Up Call 500 concurrent WebSocket connections, each holding an open SSE stream to OpenAI. My

docs.text: How I Designed an AI Chat App That Handles a Million Users (And the Mistakes That Almost Killed It). single Node.js process tried to handle 500 simultaneous TCP connections, 500 HTTP keep-alives to OpenAI, and 500 in-flight JSON serializations. It ran out of memory in 47 seconds. The Real Architecture: What a Million Users Actually Needs After the rubble settled, I rebuilt from scratch. Here's what the architecture actually looked like when we scaled to a million monthly active users. Layer 1: Connection Management (The WebSocket Problem) The first lesson: don't let application logic touch WebSocket connections directly. The WebSocket gateway is a thin, stateless layer that does one thing and does it well — maintains persistent connections. It doesn't know about models, prompts, or conversation history. It just shuttles bytes. The WebSocket breakdown: - 1 gateway node handles ~10,000 concurrent connections (8 vCPU, 16GB RAM) - At 100,000 concurrent users, you need 10 gateway nodes - Each node costs ~$80/month on AWS → $800/month for connection management Why this matters: When you have 100,000 concurrent connections and you need to restart your application server (which happens every deploy), you don't want 100,000 WebSocket reconnections. The gateway handles reconnect transparently while the app server cycles. Layer 2: Message Queuing (The LLM Latency Buffer) Here's the thing about LLMs that most system design resources won't tell you: they're slow and they're unpredictable . A GPT-4 class model generates ~30-60 tokens

During those 30-60 seconds, your entire request-response pipeline is blocked. The solution? A three-tier queue system: | Queue | Purpose | Backend | | -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------- | | Request Queue | Holds all incoming messages, ensures at-least-once delivery | Kafka / SQS | | Priority Queue | Paid users get priority routing to faster models | Redis Sorted Sets | | Stream Buffer | Buffers partial LLM responses for delivery | Redis Streams | The priority queue was a game changer. Free users enter the standard queue and get routed to the cheapest available model (Llama 3.1 8B on our own infra). Paid users get priority routing to GPT-4 or Claude. Same architecture, different queue ordering, 10x difference in perceived performance. Layer 3: LLM Routing (Where the Magic Happens) This is where most system design articles hand-wave and say "use a load balancer." Real LLM routing is harder because: 1. Models have different capabilities — GPT-4 can handle complex reasoning, a local 8B model can't 2. Costs vary by 100x — deepseek-v4-flash costs ¥0.01 per request, GPT-4 costs $1.50 3. Latency varies by model and load — a model that averages 2 seconds at noon might take 15 seconds at peak The router I built uses a

The secret? 60% of user requests are simple Q&A that a $0.0004 model handles perfectly. Layer 4: Streaming Architecture (The Hard Part) Streaming LLM responses over WebSockets sounds simple. It's not. The naive approach: The problem: LLMs don't generate tokens at a steady rate. They think for 2-3 seconds, then burst tokens at 100 tps, then slow to 20 tps, then think again. If you forward each token as a separate WebSocket frame, you create 200+ individual TCP frames per response. On 100,000 concurrent users, that's 20 million tiny frames per second — each with TCP overhead, each triggering a React re-render. The fix: batch streaming. This single change reduced WebSocket frame count by 95% and cut client-side rendering CPU usage by 60%. The trade-off? Users see text arrive in chunks instead of character-by-character. The verdict: users prefer smooth chunks over jittery character-by-character

Layer 5: Caching (The Unsung Hero) Everyone talks about caching for REST APIs. Nobody talks about caching for AI chat. There's a massive opportunity. Cache level 1: Exact prompt match (Redis) - If two users ask the exact same question, serve from cache - Hit rate: ~8% in production (users ask surprisingly similar questions about your product) - Latency saved: 2-15 seconds → 5ms Cache level 2: Semantic similarity (Vector DB) - If a user asks a question semantically similar to a previous answer, return the cached response - Uses embeddings + cosine similarity with a 0.92 threshold - Hit rate: ~15% - Risk: cached responses can be stale — needs TTL of 24 hours max Cache level 3: Prefix cache (The DeepSeek special) - DeepSeek's API caches the first N tokens of a conversation - If your system prompt is 500 tokens and a user sends a 200-token message, DeepSeek caches the first 500 tokens - Next request with the same system prompt? Only pays for the new user message - We achieved 99% cache hit rates on system prompt tokens — dropping effective cost by 60% The Three Production Incidents That Taught Me Everything Incident 1: The WebSocket Stampede (Month 3) What happened: A popular tech blog wrote about us.

Our WebSocket gateway, configured to handle 500 connections per node, received 50,000 simultaneous connection requests. Every node hit its ulimit. The ALB health checks failed. The entire cluster went down. What I learned: Never trust autoscaling to save you from a stampede. ALBs take 2-3 minutes to register new targets. By the time they spin up, the stampede is over and you're down. The fix: - Pre-provisioned connection buffer (20% over capacity at all times) - Connection rate limiter on the gateway (max 100 new connections/second/node) - Queue overflow connections with a "please wait" message instead of dropping them Incident 2: The Streaming Backpressure Disaster (Month 7) What happened: A single user with poor internet (2G connection in rural India) requested a 4000-token response. The WebSocket buffer filled up because the client couldn't consume fast enough. Instead of dropping that user's connection, the buffer grew to 200MB on the server, caused an OOM, and took down 3,000 other users' connections on the same node. What I learned: Backpressure is not optional. Every streaming system needs a flow control mechanism. The fix: - Implemented per-connection streaming windows (max 100 tokens in flight) - Added a sendStatus callback from client: {lastTokenReceived: 157} - Server pauses streaming when unacknowledged tokens exceed the window - Connection isolation —

Controversial opinion : AI coding assistants aren't just changing how we code—they're accidentally becoming the most effective therapy for impostor syndrome in tech. I know what you're thinking. "Another AI hype article?" Bear with me. This isn't about productivity gains or lines of code per minute. This is about something more fundamental: how AI made me realize I wasn't a fraud. The Setup: 5 Years of Professional Self-Doubt Picture this: 5 years into my career as a Software Engineer, working at companies like BDO Canada, shipping features used by thousands, mentoring junior developers, speaking at conferences. On paper, I was successful. In my head? I was a complete impostor. Every code review felt like an exam I hadn't studied for. Every new project felt like I was about to be exposed as someone who just got lucky. Sound familiar? Then GitHub Copilot entered my workflow six months ago. And something weird happened. The Plot Twist Nobody Saw Coming I expected AI to make me feel _more_ replaceable. Instead, it made me feel more valuable than ever. Here's why this is mind-blowing: AI Doesn't Have Ideas (But I Do) Copilot can autocomplete my functions brilliantly. It can generate boilerplate code that would take me 20 minutes in 20 seconds. But you know what it can't do? - Understand the business problem

For the first time in 8 years, I could see what I brought to the table. The "Collaboration Effect" Working with AI feels like pair programming with a really fast, really knowledgeable junior developer. And here's the kicker: when you pair program, you realize how much you actually know. Every time I had to guide Copilot's suggestions, every time I caught its mistakes, every time I provided context it couldn't understand—I was proving to myself that I wasn't just copying and pasting my way through my career. The Uncomfortable Truth About Impostor Syndrome Here's what nobody talks about: Impostor syndrome isn't just about self-doubt. It's about not understanding your own value. Most developers suffer from what I call "skill blindness"—we can't see our own expertise because we're too close to it. We focus on what we don't know (there's always more to learn) instead of acknowledging what we do know. AI acts like a skill revealer.
