docs.title: The ATS Resume That Actually Lands Interviews: A 2026 Software Engineer Guide
docs.text: The ATS Resume That Actually Lands Interviews: A 2026 Software Engineer Guide. Seventy-five percent of resumes never reach a human. Not because the candidate was unqualified, but because an algorithm said their PDF had "too many columns." You spend 12 hours tailoring a resume. Workday's parser spends 0.3 seconds deciding it's a 37% match and shoves it into the "Not Considered" bucket. You never knew you lost. You just assumed they never read it. The good news? ATS systems are stupidly predictable. They follow rigid rules. Once you know them, you can write a resume that scores well before a person ever sees it. Greenhouse's ATS ranks candidates on a 0-100 match score A resume with single-column layout, standard section headers, and high keyword overlap with the JD averages 60 points higher than one with graphics, charts, or two-column formats, even when the actual experience is identical. How ATS Actually Sees Your Resume in 2026 Most engineers think ATS systems are "AI" that understands their resume. They aren't. They're regex-and-rule engines that strip formatting, extract text, and pattern-match against job descriptions. docs.text: The 30-Year-Old 'Impossible' Algorithm That Makes Netflix Instant (And Why Your Computer Still Sucks). Netflix can tell you if a movie exists in 0.1 seconds across 15,000 titles. Your computer takes 10 seconds to find one file on your desktop. What's the difference? A probabilistic data structure called a Bloom Filter that seems to break the laws of computer science. 🤯 Mind-Blowing Fact Bloom Filters can be 99.9% accurate while using 24x less memory than traditional databases. But here's the kicker:{' '} they can lie to you... and that's exactly why they work. The Problem That Broke the Internet (Almost) Picture this: It's 2005. MySpace has 100 million users. Every second, thousands of people are trying to create accounts with usernames like "coolkid123" and "rockstar2005." Each time someone types a username, the system asks: "Is this taken?" Traditional approach? Check every single username in the database. That's like having a librarian manually flip through every book in the Library of Congress just to tell you if they have Harry Potter. The result? Servers melting. Users waiting. Companies losing millions. Enter Burton Howard Bloom, a programmer who in 1970 proposed something that sounded impossible: What if we could answer 'Is this taken?' with 99.9% accuracy, using almost no memory, and be 1000x faster than any database? His colleagues probably thought he was crazy. They were wrong. The Magic Toy Box Analogy Imagine you have a

docs.title: Building FocusTube with TypeSafe Jev
docs.text: Building FocusTube with TypeSafe Jev. YouTube is one of my best sources for programming tutorials, conference talks, and interview preparation. It is also very good at placing a Short, a product launch, or an unrelated recommendation beside the thing I opened it to learn. I wanted a stricter interface: show a recommendation only when it is clearly useful for coding, software engineering, studying, or professional upskilling. Hide everything uncertain. Do it before the card flashes on screen. That became FocusTube, an open-source Chrome and Firefox extension powered by Jev , TypeSafe AI’s first System One model. This is a small project, but it captures a useful AI engineering pattern: let the model make one semantic judgment and keep every product decision in ordinary code. The decision was the product The first version did not need summaries, generated recommendations, or a chat interface. It needed an answer to one question: Is this video directly useful for focused learning or career upskilling? A keyword list looked tempting. It also failed quickly. “React” can mean a React tutorial or a reaction video. “AI” appears in research lectures, product announcements, hype, and entertainment. A channel name helps, but it is not enough to classify every video from that channel. A general LLM could return yes or no , but then I would need to constrain and parse its response,

docs.title: Building FocusTube with TypeSafe Jev
docs.text: Building FocusTube with TypeSafe Jev. handle malformed output, and decide how much to trust an unexplained binary answer. FocusTube needed a calibrated score it could compare with a threshold. That maps directly to TypeSafe’s Noul primitive. A Noul evaluates a yes-or-no question and returns the probability that the answer is yes: No generated explanation enters the product path. 0.91 is data. The extension can reveal the card at a threshold of 0.82 , hide it at 0.61 , and let the user raise or lower that boundary. Why System One fit TypeSafe System One models are built for fast, structured decisions. Jev accepts natural-language state and returns typed answers with probabilities instead of prose and reasoning. That distinction gave each part of FocusTube one job: - Jev owns semantic judgment. It reads the title, channel, and YouTube surface and estimates whether the video fits the learning policy. - Code applies the policy. The extension defines the threshold, caching, fail-closed behavior, pause control, and which YouTube surfaces are in scope. - The browser handles presentation. Cards stay concealed until code has enough evidence to reveal them. The model is not an autonomous agent. It cannot decide to navigate, block a channel, or alter settings. Its full authority is one probability for one named question. Architecture FocusTube has two deployable pieces: a Manifest V3 extension and a

docs.text: Building FocusTube with TypeSafe Jev. Cloudflare Worker. The extension watches YouTube’s home feed, search results, and watch-page recommendations. When YouTube adds cards to the page, FocusTube: 1. Conceals each new card. 2. Extracts its title, channel, and current surface. 3. Hides Shorts locally without calling the model. 4. Checks a seven-day browser cache. 5. Sends uncached records to the Worker in batches of at most twenty. 6. Reveals only cards whose probability meets the configured threshold. The content script does not ship with a TypeSafe API key. It calls the user’s Worker with a separate extension token. The Worker validates the request, builds typed questions, calls jev-latest , and returns only the probabilities the UI needs. One state, several narrow questions TypeSafe can evaluate several questions against one state in a request. FocusTube uses that to classify a batch without turning the task into one vague, multi-video answer. The Worker sends the videos as structured state: It then creates one Noul question for each array position: The API call stays direct and inspectable: Each answer comes back under the same key as its question. The Worker maps answers.video_0.noul to the first video and returns a compact result to the extension. Strict means fail closed The default threshold is 0.82 . That number is a product control, not a claim that every result above it is

docs.text: Building FocusTube with TypeSafe Jev. correct. TypeSafe describes probabilities as calibrated across groups of predictions; an individual prediction can still be wrong. The two classification errors do not cost the same: - A false positive puts a distraction back into the feed. - A false negative hides a useful recommendation that remains available through direct navigation, subscriptions, history, or a less strict threshold. For this product, the second failure is cheaper. So an unavailable Worker, a malformed response, or a low probability keeps an unclassified card hidden. The toolbar makes the strictness visible and gives the user a pause switch when they want the original feed back. I would not reuse that policy blindly. A moderation queue, accessibility tool, or high-stakes workflow may have very different error costs. Probability is useful because application code can express those costs instead of pretending every result is equally certain. Preventing the flash of distraction Classification would feel broken if an entertainment thumbnail appeared for half a second and then vanished. The content script marks discovered cards as pending before network work starts: A MutationObserver rescans as YouTube updates its client-rendered page. Cached decisions resolve immediately. New records wait for their batch. A card receives the visible class only after its probability clears the threshold. This makes model latency less important to the interface. Users see a feed fill

docs.title: Building FocusTube with TypeSafe Jev
docs.text: Building FocusTube with TypeSafe Jev. with accepted material rather than watching rejected cards disappear. Shorts do not need AI FocusTube blocks Shorts by URL and YouTube renderer type: That check is deterministic, cheap, and more reliable than asking a model whether a known Short should be hidden. Shorts never enter a TypeSafe request. This is an important boundary when adding AI to software: use the model only where normal code cannot make the decision cleanly. DOM structure can identify a Short. Semantic relevance needs Jev. Keeping secrets outside the extension Browser extensions are distributed client code. Anything bundled with one should be treated as public. The TypeSafe API key therefore lives only in the Cloudflare Worker’s secret store. The extension uses a separate, user-configured token to authenticate to its Worker. This is not a perfect identity system—the local user can inspect their own token—but it prevents an unauthenticated public Worker URL from becoming free access to someone else’s TypeSafe quota. The Worker also enforces small input boundaries: - One to twenty videos per request - Title capped at 300 characters - Channel capped at 200 characters - Surface capped at 40 characters - Only the expected route and methods accepted FocusTube sends no YouTube cookies, account identity, watch history, comments, or transcript. The model sees the visible metadata needed for the judgment and nothing else.

docs.text: Building FocusTube with TypeSafe Jev. Caching changed both speed and cost Recommendation cards repeat. Search results reappear. YouTube can rerender the same card during navigation. Calling Jev each time would add avoidable latency and spend. The extension stores each probability in localStorage , keyed by normalized title and channel, for seven days. It caches the probability rather than the final boolean. If the user raises the threshold from 0.82 to 0.90 , FocusTube can reapply the stricter policy without another model call. There is a tradeoff: a title can change, and channel-plus-title is not a permanent video identifier. For this first version, it is available across the card types in scope and degrades safely. A future version can prefer YouTube’s video ID when every supported renderer exposes it consistently. What I would test next The repository contains a working implementation, not a published accuracy benchmark. Before treating its defaults as settled, I would create a labeled evaluation set from real recommendations and measure: 1. Precision at several thresholds, especially how much entertainment leaks through. 2. Recall for coding, system design, academic, and career-preparation subsets. 3. Disagreements around tech news, conference keynotes, and career commentary. 4. Latency and cache-hit rate across home, search, and watch sessions. 5. DOM selector breakage as YouTube changes renderers. Those results could justify separate policies by surface. Search intent may tolerate

Both are measurable changes; neither requires replacing the architecture. What this project taught me The useful part of AI here is not generated content. It is the semantic branch ordinary code could not write: Everything around that line remains conventional software engineering: narrow inputs, explicit authority, secret isolation, caching, failure policy, browser state, and a control the user can understand. That is why Jev worked well for FocusTube. It returned exactly the missing primitive—a typed judgment with a probability—and stopped there. The full extension and Worker are available in the FocusTube repository. TypeSafe’s System One documentation and API reference cover the model and response contracts used here.

docs.title: Building an MCP Server in TypeScript: From Zero to Tool-Calling Agent in 90 Minutes
docs.text: Building an MCP Server in TypeScript: From Zero to Tool-Calling Agent in 90 Minutes. TL;DR MCP is the missing layer between "an LLM that can talk" and "an LLM that can do." It is a tiny, well-designed protocol that turns any tool you already have into something Claude, Cursor, OpenCode, and a dozen other hosts can call as if it were a native function. If you can write a TypeScript function, you can ship an MCP server today. I built one in 90 minutes last weekend. This is the exact walkthrough — including the parts that bit me, the parts that surprised me, and the one architectural decision I think is going to define how agentic systems are built over the next 18 months. By the end of this post you will have: - A working MCP server with 3 tools, 2 resources, and 1 prompt - Type-safe inputs via Zod (no more "the LLM sent me garbage" debugging) - A streaming progress channel so the agent can report "I am 60% done" mid-call - A deployment path from bun run dev to a hosted endpoint anyone can install Let's go. What MCP actually is (and what it isn't) MCP — the Model Context Protocol — is Anthropic's open standard for connecting LLMs to tools. It hit 1.0 in late 2025, and the spec is refreshingly small: JSON-RPC 2.0, three primitives (tools, resources, prompts),

docs.title: Building an MCP Server in TypeScript: From Zero to Tool-Calling Agent in 90 Minutes
docs.text: Building an MCP Server in TypeScript: From Zero to Tool-Calling Agent in 90 Minutes. and a stdio or HTTP transport. That's it. What it isn't: a replacement for function calling. Your OpenAI tools= array still works. MCP is the _server_ side of that conversation. Instead of hard-coding tool definitions into every agent script you write, you publish a server, register it in your host, and every LLM that can see it gets the same capabilities. The host (Claude, Cursor, OpenCode) holds the LLM. Your TypeScript server holds the tools. They speak JSON-RPC over stdio or HTTP. The reason this matters more than "yet another API spec" is the direction of leverage . The first time you build an MCP server, you are doing it for _your_ workflow. The second time, you start noticing the same patterns — auth, rate limiting, observability — and they look like every other API you have ever built. By the third server, you realize MCP is just a really nice contract for "give an LLM a typed handle to a real-world capability." Once that clicks, the design space opens up fast. Why TypeScript, specifically I get asked this constantly. The honest answer: the SDK is most mature in TypeScript, Zod gives you runtime-validated inputs that match the LLM's JSON Schema output almost 1:1, and you almost certainly already have Node on whatever machine you are reading this on. If

docs.text: Building an MCP Server in TypeScript: From Zero to Tool-Calling Agent in 90 Minutes. you are a Python shop, the official Python SDK is fine. If you are Go or Rust, you are early. For the next 12 months, MCP server development is going to look a lot like a Node.js ecosystem in 2014 — fast-moving, full of examples, and forgiving of messy code. Step 1: Scaffold in 60 seconds That is the entire dependency tree. No express , no body-parser , no nothing. The SDK ships its own transport. No Bun? No problem. Every snippet in this post runs on Node.js 22+ via npx tsx . The starter repo ships dev:node and dev:node:http scripts as drop-in replacements. If you do not have Bun, swap bun run dev for npx tsx src/index.ts everywhere. Step 2: The 30-line server that exposes one tool This is the smallest useful MCP server I could write that still does something real — a tool that converts JSON to a TypeScript interface. Useful for exactly one workflow, and a great template to copy. server.tool() is the entire API for registering a tool. You give it a name, a description the LLM reads, a Zod schema for inputs, and an async handler. That is the whole shape. Run it: Wire it into Claude Desktop or Cursor and the LLM now has access to json_to_interface as a native capability. It will

docs.title: Building an MCP Server in TypeScript: From Zero to Tool-Calling Agent in 90 Minutes
docs.text: Building an MCP Server in TypeScript: From Zero to Tool-Calling Agent in 90 Minutes. call it, your handler runs, the response streams back, the LLM uses it. You just built an agent. Step 3: The three primitives — when to use which After about a dozen servers, the decision tree for which primitive to use stopped being obvious to me. Here is the rule I landed on: | Primitive | Use it when | Example | | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | | Tool | The LLM should _decide_ to call this based on user intent | create_issue , search_docs , deploy_preview | | Resource | The LLM should _always have access_ to this data | file://src/index.ts , db://schema | | Prompt | The user explicitly types /something to trigger a workflow | /review-pr , /release-notes , /triage | The mistake I keep seeing in early MCP servers: everything is a tool. That is wrong. Tools are for _the LLM's discretion_. If you want the LLM to always see the current branch name, expose it as a resource. If you want the user to opt in to a structured workflow, expose it as a prompt. Mixing these up is the #1 reason early MCP servers feel clunky. Step 4: The thing nobody tells you — Zod is your security boundary This is the spicy take. When an LLM calls your tool, you are

docs.title: Building an MCP Server in TypeScript: From Zero to Tool-Calling Agent in 90 Minutes
docs.text: Building an MCP Server in TypeScript: From Zero to Tool-Calling Agent in 90 Minutes. letting a model execute code in your process. Zod is not just a typescript convenience — it is the _only_ line of defense between "the model sent you what you expected" and "the model sent you { "json": "process.exit(1)" } because some prompt injection told it to." Always validate. Always narrow. Never trust the description to be enough. I learned this the hard way. I shipped a server last month where I skipped Zod on a "trust me, it's a string" field. A user pasted a JSON payload that contained a __proto__ key. My handler spread it into an options object. RCE on day one. Do not be like me. Zod everything. The 6-step request flow. Notice 95% of the latency is step 2 — the LLM itself. Your server budget is ~5ms. Spend it on validation, not optimization. Step 5: Streaming progress (the killer feature) Here is the part that surprised me most. MCP supports _progress notifications_. Your tool can stream "I am 40% done" back to the host, and the LLM can relay that to the user as it happens. This is what makes a 30-second tool feel responsive instead of broken. docs.title: Why AI Coding Agents Fail at Long Tasks (And How to Fix It)
docs.text: Why AI Coding Agents Fail at Long Tasks (And How to Fix It). 84% of multi-step agent tasks fail when they exceed 15 consecutive loops. That number should worry anyone who has watched a coding agent "work" for an hour before hallucinating an invalid state transition. The pattern is consistent across every major benchmark and production deployment: agents start strong, lose coherence as context fills, and degrade in ways that look like reasoning failures but are actually context management failures. This is the research I wish I had read before shipping my last agent pipeline. The Real Failure Mode LLMs are probabilistic text predictors, not state machines. When a multi-step task exceeds context limits, agents experience context window entropy — the model's attention becomes diluted across accumulated intermediate chatter, and state drift — the agent's internal representation of the task diverges from reality. A September 2026 ACL findings paper (StateComp) formalizes this: agents continuously accumulate interaction history during long-horizon tasks, but existing context management relies on fixed windows or passive compression heuristics. The result is context explosion, semantic drift, and degraded reasoning precisely when you need it most. The practical symptom is familiar: an agent debugging a failure can't remember the original error trace because it got compressed too early, or it carries irrelevant history that masks the real failure signal. Two Answers, Two Different Questions The 2026 work converges from two directions,

docs.title: Why AI Coding Agents Fail at Long Tasks (And How to Fix It)
docs.text: Why AI Coding Agents Fail at Long Tasks (And How to Fix It). and they are easier to apply when you keep them apart. CAT asks _what the context should contain_. StateComp asks _when it is safe to drop something_. Both train an imbalance-aware router, and both treat context maintenance as an explicit step rather than a background process. The CAT Framework Researchers at ACL 2026 proposed CAT (Context as a Tool) — a paradigm that elevates context maintenance to a callable tool integrated into the agent's decision-making process. Instead of background compression, CAT formalizes a structured context workspace with three layers: The framework trains an imbalance-aware router on hidden representations from a frozen language model. Adjacent READY interactions are grouped into continuous spans and replaced with compact summaries during execution. On SWE-Bench Verified, the resulting SWE-Compressor reached 57.6% solved rate , significantly outperforming ReAct-based agents and static compression baselines while maintaining stable long-horizon reasoning under a bounded context budget. StateComp: Compression with State Awareness StateComp takes a different angle: _when_ is a past interaction safe to replace? Premature compression removes information still needed for future actions; overly conservative retention creates massive context overhead. StateComp constructs KEEP and READY supervision through a two-stage annotation procedure and trains an imbalance-aware router. Experiments show it reduces total agent and summarization tokens by 52.27% while maintaining task performance, and achieves a 12.67× speedup in representation extraction.

docs.title: Why AI Coding Agents Fail at Long Tasks (And How to Fix It)
docs.text: Why AI Coding Agents Fail at Long Tasks (And How to Fix It). What This Means for Your Agent Architecture The 2026 Anthropic Agentic Coding Trends Report identifies multi-agent coordination and human-AI collaboration patterns as the top foundation trends for the year. But the engineering reality is simpler: before you orchestrate agent teams, you need each individual agent to maintain coherence over long tasks. The Uncomfortable Tradeoff There is a tension between agent autonomy and reliability that no model update solves. More capable models delay the failure but don't prevent it — 84% failure on 15+ loop tasks is a structural problem, not a capability gap. The agents that succeed in production are not the ones with the best model. They are the ones with the best context management. The research is clear: treat context as a tool, not a container. Your agent's coherence depends on it. Sources - StateComp: Learning When to Compress History in Long Horizon Agents — ACL 2026 findings paper on state-conditioned compression - Context as a Tool: Context Management for Long-Horizon SWE-Agents — CAT framework and SWE-Compressor benchmarks - 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report — Anthropic's eight trends for agentic coding - Why AI Agents Fail on Long Coding Tasks — Practical breakdown of context window entropy and state drift - SWE-Bench Verified — Benchmark for long-horizon software engineering agents

docs.title: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook
docs.text: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook. Event-driven architecture replaces time-based scheduling with intent-based scheduling. When work is scheduled by the clock, the system develops a hidden class of bugs — missed windows, cascading retries, daylight-saving surprises, and silent partial state — that don't exist when work is scheduled by the fact that caused it. This post is the playbook for moving a real production system from cron to an event bus without breaking it. --- The incident that proved it It was a Tuesday at 11:47 PM UTC. A reconciliation cron — the kind that's been quietly doing its job for three years — failed on a network timeout. The retry kicked in. It hit the same timeout. The retry kicked in again. By the time anyone noticed, the cron had retried 47 times in a 90-minute window, hammering the downstream database with the same query. The interesting part isn't that the cron failed. Cron fails all the time. The interesting part is the _shape_ of the failure: it wasn't a one-off bug, it was a class of bug that the architecture itself made easy to produce. The clock kept ticking; the retries had no notion of _intent_; the downstream system had no way to deduplicate what it was receiving. Three weeks later, after a finance reconciliation caught a different silent failure — a state change

docs.title: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook
docs.text: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook. that hadn't propagated to a downstream consumer because the cron had been running on stale assumptions — the team made the call. We're not fixing this cron. We're replacing the model. This is the playbook for what came next. The starting state: cron sprawl Here's what the system looked like before. If you've ever inherited a few years of "just one more cron," it will look familiar. The numbers from this system: - 47 cron entries spread across 6 services - 5 cron entries with implicit ordering dependencies (a billing-svc cron assumed a webhook-svc cron had already run) - 3 distinct time zones in the cron expressions (UTC, America/Toronto, Europe/Berlin) — at least one was wrong - ~6 hours per month spent babysitting: investigating missed runs, replaying logs, manually triggering retries - 3 incidents in the past quarter traceable to missed windows or retry storms Cron wasn't a bad decision when it was made. It was the simplest thing that could work, and it worked for a long time. That's not a sin — that's how software grows. The problem is that cron accumulates . Each new entry added another implicit dependency, and the system wasn't designed — it accumulated. Why event-driven, and why now Three things changed: 1. Scale : crons that took 5 minutes started taking 45 minutes.

docs.title: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook
docs.text: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook. The reconciliation cron, when it finally worked, blocked four downstream consumers from processing fresh data for almost an hour. 2. Observability ceiling : there was no way to answer "what ran, in what order, with what result?" by grepping cron logs. The information existed in 47 different files, written by 6 different services, in 3 different log formats. 3. Incident count : missed windows + cascading retries + a daylight-saving bug that fired a job twice in one hour pushed the team past a threshold. The decision wasn't "cron is bad." The decision was " for jobs where the real trigger was never the clock, we were polling on a timer because that was the only tool we had ." The decision matrix A quick one — not exhaustive, but enough to think with: | Trigger type | Use when | Watch out for | | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | | Cron / scheduled | Reports, reconciliation, digests, anything genuinely calendar-driven | DST, missed windows, retry storms, ordering assumptions | | Queue | Tasks that should run once, with retries | Poison messages, ordering, backpressure | | Event bus | Things that should happen _because_ something else happened | Idempotency, schema evolution, observability across services | The honest version of the playbook: migrate the host for every job,

docs.title: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook
docs.text: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook. migrate the trigger model only for jobs where time was a proxy for an event. Time is sometimes the right trigger — a monthly billing reconciliation is a time-based fact, and forcing it into events buys you nothing. The migration design Four contracts make this safe. Get any one wrong and the migration will silently corrupt state. The point of this section isn't "use Pact." The point is: when you cut over a producer and a consumer to a new boundary, you need a way to prove the boundary is what both sides think it is. Without it, every cutover is a leap of faith. The other two contracts — schema versioning (so producers can't break consumers silently) and observability (every event carries a trace ID, so you can correlate across services) — are covered well elsewhere. The pattern matters more than the tool: don't ship the migration without these four contracts in place. The cutover plan Four phases. The most common mistake is collapsing phases 1 and 2; don't. | Phase | What happens | What proves it's safe to move on | | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 1. Shadow | New consumer reads events from the bus, logs what it _would_ do, takes no action | Shadow consumer's output matches cron output for 7 days

docs.title: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook
docs.text: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook. straight, in production traffic | | 2. Dual-write | Producer emits both to the old cron path AND the new bus; both run, neither is authoritative | The diff between cron results and bus results is empty across 14 days | | 3. Dark launch | Event bus is authoritative; cron still runs but its output is discarded | Customers see no change in behavior for 14 days; incident count doesn't increase | | 4. Cron disabled | Cron entries deleted, alerts cleaned up, runbooks updated | One full quarter with zero cron-driven incidents in this category | The phase that always takes 3x as long as estimated is phase 3 , and the bottleneck is never code. It's coordination: getting every team that depends on the cron's side effects to agree on the cutover date, getting the runbook updated, getting the alerts retargeted at the new metric. The engineering is the easy part. A note on rollback : every phase has to be rollback-able in under 15 minutes. That means the dual-write phase has to be able to disable the bus path instantly without touching the cron path, and vice versa. If you can't roll back in 15 minutes, you're not ready to move on. The three-week bug hunt The bug that justified the entire migration slipped through every

docs.title: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook
docs.text: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook. test we'd written. In the dual-write phase, we shipped the most natural-looking producer you can imagine: This passed the contract test. It passed the shadow consumer. It passed the dual-write diff. It failed in production for a reason none of those tests covered. Here's what happened: the customer-facing cancel endpoint committed the subscription status change at T+0ms. The bus event landed at T+1ms. The cron reconciliation — still running during dual-write — fired at T+200ms, queried the database (now in the post-cancel state), and concluded "nothing to cancel." But the cron reconciliation had its own ordering assumptions: it expected a downstream notification service to be in a particular state, and that state depended on the bus event being fully processed. The bus event _had_ been processed. But the reconciliation cron's notion of "processed" was based on its own query, not on the bus's offset tracking. The two drifted. Three weeks later, a finance reconciliation caught that we'd sent "your subscription was cancelled" emails to customers whose accounts were still active — and _also_ failed to send them to customers whose accounts were correctly cancelled, because the cron's state read was racing with the bus's offset commit. The fix wasn't a one-line patch. It was the transactional outbox pattern : The lesson is sharper than "use the outbox pattern." The lesson

docs.title: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook
docs.text: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook. is: dual-write is correct in principle and dangerous in practice. Without the transactional outbox, you have a race window between the event emit and the state commit. With it, you have a durable queue that can never get ahead of — or behind — your state. The pattern is one of the most-cited tools in this canonical Stripe writeup on idempotency, and it's worth the read in full if you're going to do a migration like this. What I'd do differently Three concrete lessons, not platitudes. 1. Underestimate coordination, not engineering. The engineering for this migration was about 25% of the calendar time. The other 75% was coordinating across teams — getting sign-off on cutover dates, updating runbooks, retargeting alerts, getting finance to agree on what "reconciliation passed" means. If I'd modeled the project realistically, I'd have budgeted 6 engineers for 6 months, not 3 engineers for 4 months. I've written before about how I underestimated migration timelines for a database move — same lesson, different stack. 2. Add the transactional outbox from day one. I would not do a dual-write phase without the outbox in place from the first commit. We added it after the three-week bug hunt. The cost of the bug hunt was larger than the cost of building the outbox first. A senior+ reader I respect

docs.title: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook
docs.text: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook. has written about similar migration patterns for legacy codebases that reinforce this — the migration shape you start with shapes the failure modes you discover. 3. Cut anything that isn't moving state or shaping the cutover. The plan we shipped had three deliverables that turned out to be pure overhead: a "migration dashboard" (nobody read it), a "weekly stakeholder update" (three weeks in, everyone stopped opening it), and a "rollback dry-run" (we never ran it; we ran a real rollback once and that was the test). If you're planning a similar migration, your three deliverables should be: contract tests, the outbox, and the cutover playbook. Everything else is decoration. docs.text: Running a Coding Agent on DeepSeek V4 Flash: The 1M-Context Cheap Workhorse. My coding agent talks to deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731 through OpenRouter, and the single most unbelievable number about that setup is not the model's benchmark score. It is the price of the average turn. Most coding-agent turns cost me roughly a fraction of a US cent . Not a third of a cent of a bundled subscription, not a rounded-up estimate. A fraction of a cent, measured from the billed token counts. Several hours of continuous autonomous work can run lower than a single cup of coffee. That is only possible because of three unrelated facts stacking together: a one-million-token context window , DeepSeek's prefix caching , and per-token pricing of $1 input / $2 output / $0.02 cache-hit per million tokens. This post is a practical field note about what those numbers mean when you actually operate an agent, not a benchmark. If you want leaderboard scores, this is the wrong place—I am not going to invent any. What the actual numbers look like Here is the real pricing sheet I work against, stated as a fixed unit of one million tokens: | Direction | Price per 1M tokens | | --------------------------------- | ------------------: | | Input (cache miss / fresh prompt) | $1.00 | | Output (generation) | $2.00 | | Input (cache hit) | $0.02 | The model identifier is

It exposes a 1,000,000-token context window , and it is the cheap, fast tier in my setup—paired with a heavier deepseek-pro tier that I route hard tasks to. The gap that makes the whole thing work is the one at the bottom of the table. A cache hit costs fifty times less than a fresh input token. In a long agent session, almost every token you send is a cache hit, because the agent keeps resending the same large prefix over and over. Here is the same snippet as a cut-and-paste curl , if you want to poke at the fields yourself: One million tokens is a lot. It is on the order of a small repository's entire source tree, or an entire afternoon of agent conversation, retained in one window. What a one-million-token window actually buys you Most coding agents spend their lives fighting a small context. With a 128k or 200k window, you start every task by deciding what to discard: the repo map, the older conversation, the tool output you might still need. Getting this wrong produces the classic agent failure mode where the model forgets what it decided two turns ago and redoes the work. With a million tokens, that whole class of problem mostly disappears. - Whole-repo context fits. For

A long multi-step debugging run no longer needs to be compressed into an ever-shrinking summary that quietly drops the important constraints. - Fewer compactions. The agent jargon for this is "context compaction"—rewriting the conversation into a shorter summary to free space. Every compaction is a small information-loss at best and a self-inflicted bug at worst. A larger window means far fewer of them. The practical effect is that the agent stops spending effort on memory management and starts spending it on the actual task. That sounds vague until you watch a session run for hours without once asking "wait, why am I doing this again?" It just keeps its own thread of reasoning in front of it. There is a real cost to a huge window, and I will be honest about it. Context is not free to compute. Prefill—reading and processing all those cached tokens—takes time even when the tokens are cheap. For a long session you trade per-turn latency for the absence of compaction mistakes. On Flash, that trade lands in the right place; on the slower pro tier it is a reason to be more disciplined about trimming. Why prefix caching changes

docs.text: Running a Coding Agent on DeepSeek V4 Flash: The 1M-Context Cheap Workhorse. the cost model This is the part most people misunderstand. They read "$1 input / $2 output" and conclude a long agent session is expensive, because they picture every turn paying full input price for the whole conversation. That picture is wrong, and it is wrong in the way that matters most. A coding agent does not send fresh tokens each turn. It sends the same long prefix—system prompt, repo context, conversation history—and appends only the newest piece. DeepSeek's prefix caching recognizes that the front of the prompt is unchanged and serves the cached portion at $0.02 per million tokens instead of $1. Here is the arithmetic for a typical turn with, say, 400k tokens of shared prefix and 2k tokens of new output: Twelve thousandths of a cent. That is the "fraction of a cent per turn" I opened with. The critical variable is the cache-hit rate . In my long agent sessions, Piyush observes ~99% of input tokens come back as cache hits. At that rate the effective input price collapses toward a rounding error, and the dominant cost of a session becomes—surprisingly—the tiny output tokens it actually generates. That changes design decisions. When input tokens are nearly free, you stop being stingy with context. You happily re-send the whole repo map every turn, because resending is cheaper

The economics of the agent flip from "minimize tokens sent" to "send plenty, but keep the prefix stable so it stays cached." The one thing that breaks the math is changing the prefix. The moment an earlier part of the conversation changes—say, a tool result gets rewritten out of place—the cache invalidates from that point on, and you pay full input price again for everything after. A well-behaved agent keeps history immutable and only ever appends. Flash versus pro: the routing tradeoff The 1M-context Flash model is not a replacement for harder models. It is the cheap, fast tier in a two-model setup, and the other half is deepseek-pro , which I use for the jobs Flash handles poorly. The practical rule I landed on is a routing split by task shape: | Task shape | Tier | | ---------------------------------------------- | ----- | | Repetitive file edits, refactors, boilerplate | Flash | | Long multi-file searches across a big repo | Flash | | Reading and summarizing lots of cached context | Flash | | Hard algorithmic reasoning | Pro | | Debugging subtle concurrency or state bugs | Pro | | Ambiguous tool-use sequences that need care | Pro | Routing matters for two reasons. That density of cheap iterations is where agent productivity compounds—you can afford to try a change, look at the diff, and try again. Second, it keeps the expensive model from being wasted. If deepseek-pro costs an order of magnitude more, you do not want it regenerating a boilerplate component when Flash can do that all day for pocket change. You want Pro for the one or two genuinely hard steps in a session, not the dozen easy ones around them. The honest caveat is that this split is not automatic. It requires a router that looks at the task and picks a tier, and routing mistakes are costly in both directions: sending hard work to Flash produces bad output, and sending easy work to Pro burns money and adds latency. Getting the routing heuristic right is the difference between a budget that feels free and one that quietly bleeds. docs.text: Running a Coding Agent on DeepSeek V4 Flash: The 1M-Context Cheap Workhorse. bottom line: what 1M context plus cheap input actually unlocks Stepping back, the thing that surprised me most is not any single number. It is how the numbers combine into a different kind of agent. One million tokens of context means the agent can carry a whole repo and a whole session without constantly forgetting. Prefix caching at $0.02 input means carrying that context is nearly free. Together they make a coding agent that is not thrifty and nervous about tokens, but relaxed and persistent—the kind that will keep digging for an hour because another turn is basically free. The setup still punches above its weight class only when you respect its limits. Use it for the long, repetitive, search-heavy work where its cheap iterations and huge context shine. Route the genuinely hard reasoning elsewhere. Keep your session prefixes stable so the cache keeps hitting. Do those three things and the math stops being a novelty and starts being a working habit: a capable agent, running all day, at a fraction of a cent per meaningful step. That is the real takeaway. The interesting question about a cheap 1M-context model is not "is it as smart as the frontier?" It is "what can you afford to run continuously that you never could before?" docs.text: The First 90 Days At A New Software Engineering Job: A Week-By-Week Playbook. 30% of new hires fail their first 90 days. And 70% of those failures get decided in week one. I've started three new software engineering roles across a late-stage startup, Big Tech, and fintech. I bombed the first onboarding badly enough that my manager asked if I was "having second thoughts." I crushed the next two so thoroughly that by day 60 I was the person new joiners were told to go to for help. The difference wasn't coding ability. It was having a repeatable 90-day system. 30% of new hires leave within their first 90 days A BambooHR study of 10,000+ employees found that for software engineers, it climbs to 35% when onboarding lacks structure. Your first week isn't a soft ramp. It's a flight that decides whether you crash or land. Why Your First 90 Days Matter More Than Your Last 90 Managers form a permanent impression in the first 1-2 weeks. That's the primacy effect in organizational psychology. Everything after that just confirms or revises that snapshot. Here's what makes the honeymoon period uniquely powerful: - The team expects you to ask questions. docs.text: GPT-6.1 Sol vs Astra: 5× Cheaper, But Is It Good Enough?. Your spreadsheet wants GPT-6.1 Sol. Your production incident wants proof. OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol announcement makes a compelling pitch: near-Astra intelligence for coding, computer use, and professional work at one-fifth of Astra's standard API input and output token prices. The important word is near . That is OpenAI's positioning, not a guarantee that Sol will match Astra on your repository or your agent's tasks. For developers, the interesting question is whether the quality difference is small enough to justify the price difference. The Sol model documentation explicitly recommends comparing the two on your own work. What the prices actually say At standard API rates, the published Sol prices and Astra prices are: - Input, per million tokens: Sol $2; Astra $10. - Cached input, per million tokens: Sol $0.10; Astra $1. - Output, per million tokens: Sol $10; Astra $50. The one-fifth comparison applies to uncached input and output , not every line item. Cached input is one-tenth Astra's listed rate. Sol also lists cache writes at $2.50 per million tokens, versus $12.50 for Astra. For a request with 100,000 uncached input tokens and 20,000 output tokens, those rates imply about $0.40 on Sol versus $2 on Astra , before any tool fees. That is a pricing illustration, not a measured workload or a prediction of how many tokens either model

docs.text: GPT-6 Luna Decisions: Typed Probabilities for Real Support Routing. OpenAI released the Decisions API in public beta on October 6, 2026, powered by GPT-6 Luna. You may see it listed as gpt-6-luna-decisions by model routers. The interesting part isn't another chat model with a new name. It's a different API surface: give it evidence and typed questions, and get back decisions your application can consume. That distinction matters for support teams. A chatbot can write, “This looks like a billing issue.” A routing system needs a queue name, a probability, and a policy for what to do when the evidence is weak. Luna Decisions is designed to return the former as structured data. Your code still owns the latter. What the Decisions API does The public-beta Decisions API evaluates text, images, or both. Its documented endpoint is POST /v1/decisions , and gpt-6-luna is the model currently documented for it. A request contains a model, shared input, and one or more named questions. The question types include predicate, choice, and score. Those types let you ask whether a condition holds, select from a fixed set, or rate evidence against a rubric. OpenAI describes this endpoint as returning typed answers and says it is about 10x faster than the Responses API. That's the vendor's comparison, not an independent benchmark or a promise for every workload. The API is in public beta,

The important separation is between a model answer and an application decision. A returned probability is useful evidence; it isn't a service-level guarantee, a calibrated confidence interval, or permission to skip review. Choose thresholds based on measured performance on your own ticket mix. The three question types map to different kinds of work. A predicate is useful for a yes-or-no check, such as whether a message describes an account lockout. A choice fits routing because the allowed destinations are explicit. A score fits a rubric, such as urgency on a defined scale. You can ask more than one named question over the same input, which can avoid sending the same ticket through several separate model calls. Keep each question narrow enough that a support lead can explain what a correct answer means. Why use it for support triage? Consider a ticket that says, “My renewal went through, but the dashboard still says trial.” A conversational model might produce a thoughtful explanation and ask follow-up questions. But before any reply, your help desk needs to know where the ticket belongs. Ask for one choice from a small set: billing , account_access , or technical_support . The threshold is a policy knob owned by the product team, not a magic number emitted by the model. A stricter threshold trades more manual review for fewer uncertain automatic assignments. Start conservative, sample decisions, and adjust after reviewing real outcomes. A direct API request The example below uses the public Decisions endpoint, not a chat-completions route. Keep the API key on a server and supply it through an environment variable. The question constrains the answer to a fixed choice set, while the ticket text remains the evidence. Use a unique question name so you can associate each answer with the matching question. Choices are objects with a value and description , not an array of strings. For a real ticket, pass only the text needed to make the decision, and follow your normal privacy and retention rules. docs.text: Herdr Is the Runtime Your Coding Agents Live On. I closed the lid, drove to a coffee shop, and the agent that had been refactoring a two-hundred-file monorepo for ninety minutes was still running when I opened it back up. The terminal was sitting in the same pane, the same scrollback, the same place in the diff. The only thing that had changed was the Wi-Fi network. The thing that had been quietly killing me was not the answer the agent eventually produced. It was the ninety minutes it had been working while I was not, and the five minutes I would have spent restarting it every time the laptop slept. Coding agents are good now. They run for hours. They refactor whole trees, they run test suites, they wait on pull-request reviews. The bottleneck, again, was not the model. It was the terminal. Herdr is the runtime that makes this routine. It is a single Rust binary that holds your coding agents' terminals open across laptop closes, network drops, and machine restarts — and tells you, without you to clicking, which one is stuck. After a few weeks it has changed how I think about agent work entirely. The short version: Herdr is one Rust binary that keeps your coding agents' terminals alive when the laptop sleeps, the SSH drops, and the Wi-Fi changes — and twenty agents

docs.text: Herdr Is the Runtime Your Coding Agents Live On. show up the moment you install it. Why every agent session is a borrowed process Here is the part that was wearing me down. A coding agent runs in a terminal. A terminal belongs to a TTY. A TTY dies when the SSH session drops, when the lid closes, when the laptop sleeps, when the Wi-Fi flips to a captive portal, when the user's shell exits because they closed their emulator. Every "session" for an agent is a borrowed process. The agent is a tenant in someone else's house, and the landlord can evict it any time. The hidden cost of that eviction is not the lost compute. It is the lost context. The agent had read the diff, planned the refactor, hit the first migration, decided to keep the old behavior for the second one, and was halfway through the third. The eviction kills the reasoning, not the work — and the model has to start the reasoning over. I do not want a desktop Electron app to manage my agents. I do not want a hosted SaaS IDE. I want the terminal to keep being the terminal, and I want the agents to keep being the agents, and I want neither of them to be at the mercy of my lid. The author of Herdr described the same

docs.title: Kimi K3 Is Open Weight, but You Still Need a Datacenter to Run It
docs.text: Kimi K3 Is Open Weight, but You Still Need a Datacenter to Run It. Moonshot AI just put one of the largest AI model checkpoints ever released on Hugging Face. You can download it without asking for API access, waiting for an enterprise contract, or trusting that a model provider will keep the same endpoint alive next year. There is only one small problem: the download is 1.56 terabytes . That number is not an estimate from a launch slide. I counted the 96 .safetensors weight shards in the official Hugging Face repository and summed their published file sizes: 1,560,936,091,448 bytes . On a connection sustaining a full 1 Gbps, the weights alone would take about three and a half hours to transfer. At 100 Mbps, the theoretical minimum is almost 35 hours. Storing the files is the easy part. Kimi K3 has 2.8 trillion total parameters , activates 104 billion parameters for each token , supports a 1,048,576-token context window , and uses native visual input. Moonshot's own deployment guidance recommends a supernode with 64 or more accelerators . So yes, Kimi K3 is open weight. No, it is not a laptop model. That apparent contradiction is the most important part of this release. Kimi K3 does not put frontier intelligence on every desk. It changes who is allowed to operate it, preserve it, modify it, study it, and sell access to it.

docs.text: Kimi K3 Is Open Weight, but You Still Need a Datacenter to Run It. The gatekeeper moves from permission to compute . The Kimi K3 paradox The weights are open enough to download, restricted enough to have a revenue clause, and large enough that most developers will still rent access from somebody else. This is not a hands-on model review. Launch-day API comparisons would be misleading without the same harness, reasoning budget, tool environment, and repeated runs. This is an evidence audit of what Moonshot released on July 27, 2026, what the architecture means, what the license permits, what independent evaluation has established, and why weights that almost nobody can run locally still matter. What Moonshot actually released The headline is the full model checkpoint, but the release is larger than a directory full of tensors. Moonshot published: - the Kimi K3 weights and model card; - a detailed technical report; - a custom Kimi K3 license; - recipes for serving the model with vLLM, SGLang, and TokenSpeed; - FlashKDA, MIT-licensed CUDA kernels for Kimi Delta Attention; - MoonEP, an MIT-licensed expert-parallel communication library; and - AgentENV, an MIT-licensed distributed system for running and resuming agent sandboxes at scale. That surrounding infrastructure matters. A model architecture is useful only if somebody can execute it efficiently. Kimi Delta Attention needs specialized kernels. A sparse model with hundreds of experts needs a way to route tokens across accelerators without one overloaded expert slowing every other device. Long-running coding agents need environments that can pause, resume, fork, and retain filesystem state. The release therefore exposes three different layers: The weights receive the headlines. The infrastructure determines whether the weights become a usable ecosystem rather than a 1.56 TB museum exhibit. There are still important things Moonshot did not release. The complete pre-training dataset is not available.

The report describes training methods, reinforcement-learning environments, and infrastructure, but it is not a fully reproducible recipe that lets another lab recreate K3 from raw data. Open weights give outsiders the trained artifact; they do not expose every decision that produced it. How can a 2.8-trillion-parameter model use only 104 billion parameters? Kimi K3 is a Mixture of Experts , or MoE, model. The simplest way to understand MoE is to separate the model's total knowledge capacity from the amount of machinery used for one token. A conventional dense model uses essentially the same parameter blocks for every token. An MoE model contains many specialized feed-forward blocks called experts. A router scores those experts and sends each token through only a small subset. K3 has 896 routed experts. It selects 16 for each token, with two additional shared experts. The routed fraction is only about 1.8% of the expert pool at a time. This is why both of these statements can be true: 1. Kimi K3 contains 2.8 trillion parameters. 2. It activates 104 billion—about 3.7% of the total —for a token. The benefit is sparse computation. K3 can increase total model capacity without paying the arithmetic cost of a dense 2.8T model on every token. But sparse computation is not sparse ownership. The router can choose different experts for

docs.text: Kimi K3 Is Open Weight, but You Still Need a Datacenter to Run It. the next token, request, or user. All expert weights must remain available somewhere in the serving system. You cannot keep only today's 16 experts and delete the remaining 880; the next token may need a different combination. A restaurant analogy helps, as long as we do not stretch it too far. One meal may use only 16 specialists, but the restaurant still needs the full kitchen because the next order can require another team. MoE reduces how many cooks touch one plate. It does not shrink the building. Three architectural ideas behind K3 MoE is only one part of the design. The report organizes K3 around information flow across sequence length, network depth, and model width. 1. Kimi Delta Attention across sequence length. KDA is a recurrent, linear-attention mechanism intended to process long sequences more efficiently than applying full quadratic attention at every layer. K3 interleaves three KDA layers with one Gated Multi-head Latent Attention layer. The periodic global-attention layers retain unrestricted token-to-token interaction. 2. Attention Residuals across depth. A conventional residual stream repeatedly accumulates each layer's output. Attention Residuals let a layer selectively retrieve representations from earlier blocks instead of accepting the entire history with equal weight. Think of it as giving depth its own retrieval mechanism. 3. Stable LatentMoE across width. K3 scales to 896 routed experts while

MoonEP addresses a related systems problem: if too many tokens select experts on one accelerator, that device becomes the bottleneck. Its dynamic redundant-expert design aims to keep the work balanced across ranks. Moonshot says these changes, together with its training and data recipes, deliver roughly 2.5 times better scaling efficiency than Kimi K2 . That wording matters. It is a company-reported scaling-law result about capability gained per training compute. It does not mean K3 is automatically 2.5 times faster or cheaper to serve. Why a sparse model still weighs 1.56 TB K3 uses quantization-aware training with MXFP4 weights and MXFP8 activations . Four-bit weights are a major reason a 2.8T-parameter checkpoint can fit into roughly 1.56 TB rather than several terabytes more. Yet four bits multiplied by 2.8 trillion parameters is already about 1.4 TB before accounting for scales, metadata, non-weight files, and format overhead. Compression makes the release possible. It does not make it small. The runtime also needs more than static weight storage: - memory for active computations; - recurrent and attention state; - buffers for expert routing and cross-device communication; - image representations for multimodal requests; - cache or state for long conversations; - and capacity for concurrent users. The advertised one-million-token context window makes the systems problem harder. Maximum

docs.text: Kimi K3 Is Open Weight, but You Still Need a Datacenter to Run It. context is not free memory, instant prefill, or perfect recall. A provider must ingest the prompt, maintain the model's state, schedule work, and decide what can be cached. Long agent sessions also branch, call tools, retry failed actions, and append large tool outputs. Moonshot's official blog recommends deploying K3 on supernode configurations with 64 or more accelerators because inference benefits from a large high-bandwidth communication domain. That is a recommendation, not a formally published minimum. Creative operators will try slower storage offloading, unusual quantizations, fewer devices, and expert streaming. The trade-off will be latency, throughput, context capacity, or all three. The early r/LocalLLaMA launch thread captured the problem perfectly. The most popular joke was: "How do I download RAM in Hugging Face?" Underneath the joke were serious debates about multi-node B200/B300 systems, storage capacity, tokens per second, and whether self-hosting could ever beat paying an inference provider. Those comments are useful signals, not benchmark data. Hardware prices and throughput estimates posted during launch-day excitement should not be repeated as facts without measured deployments. The reliable conclusion is narrower: K3 is datacenter-class software today. The more precise description is open weight with a custom license . The Kimi K3 License grants broad rights to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, sell, deploy, and fine-tune the software and weights. It then adds commercial conditions that standard permissive licenses such as MIT or Apache 2.0 do not contain. The two conditions most businesses need to notice are: 1. Inference providers can compete with the creator A closed model has one official seller. The provider controls price, regions, rate limits, retention policies, safety behavior, and deprecation. Open weights allow independent operators to compete on: - price per token; - latency and geographic location; - privacy and data residency; - context limits; - quantization; - fine-tuning; - tool-use policies; and - service reliability. Most developers may still call an API, but they no longer have to call one specific API . Moonshot's official service launched at $0.30 per million cache-hit input tokens, $3 per million cache-miss input tokens, and $15 per million output tokens . Those prices are a snapshot, not a permanent property of the model. Once more providers deploy K3, the market can test how much of that price reflects compute, utilization, software quality, or margin. 2. It is also why releasing capable weights creates a different security profile from exposing the same model through a monitored API. docs.text: Mellum2.1 and the Local Coding Agent Test That Actually Matters. A model that can write a function is not necessarily a model that can repair a repository. The latter has to find the right file, avoid unrelated edits, run the right test, and stop when it has enough evidence. That is the interesting question behind JetBrains' October 8 release of Mellum2.1, a 12B-total-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 2.5B active parameters, released under Apache 2.0. JetBrains says the architecture stayed the same as Mellum2; most of the change was post-training, including reinforcement learning in repositories with shell and file-editing tools. On its model card, JetBrains reports 47.0% on SWE-bench Verified for Mellum2.1 Thinking, versus 2.0% for Mellum2 Thinking , using its own evaluation pipeline. That is a striking _vendor-reported_ difference, not a prediction that 47% of your issues will be fixed. The card specifies a shared Pi v0.73.1 harness with shell/file tools, 114K context, up to 16K tokens per turn, and each model's default sampling. Change the harness, task mix, or time budget and the comparison changes too. The useful takeaway isn't “switch models.” It's test the entire worker, not just the model . A local agent may be an excellent cheap first pass for a narrow, well-tested job; it might be the wrong choice for a migration spanning five services. Hide the solution commits from the candidate's workspace, but retain them for grading. Include at least one issue requiring navigation across files and one where the first plausible fix is wrong. Run every candidate from the same base commit in an isolated worktree or disposable container, with the same tool permissions and time/token budget. No network or production credentials unless the task truly requires them. For each run, record: 1. Outcome: did the original failing test pass, and did the full relevant suite remain green? A passing suite alone can miss an incomplete fix; compare behavior against the issue's acceptance criteria. 2. Scope: how many files changed outside the expected area? Inspect the diff, including test deletions and config changes. 3. Intervention: did a human have to redirect the agent, repair its patch, or select a different tool? 4. Cost and latency: measure wall time, tokens if exposed, and peak memory for the _whole agent run_. “2.5B active” is not a hardware-memory specification: the model has 12B total parameters, plus runtime overhead and KV cache. 5. Reproducibility: repeat a couple of tasks with another seed or run. One lucky patch isn't a reliable routing policy. Keep a holdout issue outside the tuning set. Never compare two models with different file access and then attribute the result solely to weights. A routing decision you can practice You have a local worker with read/write access to a disposable worktree. Which task gets an _automated candidate patch_ first? Open a case, make your call, then read the tradeoff. Case A: A utility function fails on empty input; the regression test already exists Good first candidate. Give the agent the failing test and a bounded file scope. Accept only a patch that passes that test and the surrounding suite; review the diff. Small blast radius, cheap oracle. Case B: Rotate production signing keys across three services with no integration tests Do not auto-route. The absence of a reliable oracle and the credential blast radius dominate model speed. First design the rollout and rollback with a human owner, then delegate isolated implementation pieces in a credential-free sandbox. Case C: A flaky integration test passes locally but fails in CI Investigate first. Ask the worker to collect hypotheses and evidence without changing files. A green local run isn't evidence that the CI race is fixed. Reproduce the failure under the relevant CI conditions before accepting a patch. This isn't a vendor-specific flow. docs.title: What the Hell is microfrontend?
docs.text: What the Hell is microfrontend?. The term Micro Frontends first came up in ThoughtWorks Technology Radar at the end of 2016. Micro-frontend architecture is a design approach in which a front-end app is decomposed into individual, semi-independent “microapps” working loosely together. This concept is vaguely inspired by, and named after, microservices. The concept of Micro Frontend Architecture is to think about a web application as a composition of features owned by different independent teams. Each team having a distinct area of business that it specializes in. The current trend is to build a feature-rich and powerful browser application, aka single page app, which sits on top of a micro service architecture. Over time the frontend layer, often developed by a separate team, grows and gets more difficult to maintain. That’s what we call a Frontend Monolith. The benefits of the micro-frontend pattern include 1. Micro-frontend architectures may be simpler, and thus easier to reason about and manage. 1. Independent development teams can collaborate on a front-end app more easily. 1. They can provide a means for migrating from an “old” app by having a “new” app running side by side with it. Best Practices of Micro-Frontend 1. The Single-SPA meta-framework to combine multiple frameworks on the same page without refreshing the page such a React, Vue, Angular 1, Angular 2 etc. 1. docs.text: npm Trusted Publishing Now Moves dist-tags: Delete Your Last NPM_TOKEN. You have removed NPM_TOKEN from the publish job. A release lands under next ; tests pass; now someone needs to point latest at that version. The promotion job still has a token in GitHub Secrets. You fixed the publish credential but left the release switch behind. As of September 30, 2026, npm trusted publisher configurations can opt into Allow npm dist-tag . The permission is off by default and independent of direct publishing. A workflow can use its short-lived OIDC identity to move a tag rather than keep a long-lived token for that last step. Existing token-based flows continue to work; nothing migrates automatically. Why care about one leftover token? Because stolen npm credentials are how the Shai-Hulud worm spread in September 2025: it harvested secrets, authenticated to npm as the compromised developer, and published infected versions of their other packages. CISA counted more than 500 compromised packages. A long-lived token that can only move latest is a smaller prize than a publish token, but it can still repoint every fresh install of your package to a version you did not intend. The interesting engineering decision is not whether to tick the box. It is which workflow gets to move latest . TL;DR - Enable Allow npm dist-tag only on the trusted publisher for your _promotion_ workflow. It is off

GitHub's announcement and npm's trusted publisher documentation spell out these rules. A separate workflow file is not by itself an approval boundary. Restrict who can edit and run it, use a protected GitHub environment where appropriate, and validate that the requested version is the one you intended to promote. docs.text: Python 3.10 End of Life: A Practical Upgrade Guide for 2026. Your application still starts. Your tests still pass. The Docker image still builds. None of those things tell you whether the interpreter underneath it will receive another security fix. Python 3.10 reached end of life on October 1, 2026. The official release announcement names 3.10.22 as its final release and says the series will receive no further security updates. Installing that final patch does not extend its support window. This is the useful question behind the release news: which Python actually runs your application, who maintains it, and how do you replace it without guessing about compatibility? The short answer: Inventory deployed interpreters, choose a supported target your dependencies can run on, recreate environments, then test and roll out a new artifact. Updating packages with pip does not update Python. The support table below is a snapshot checked on October 5, 2026 , not a permanent promise about which patch is latest. What changed in the October Python releases? The October 1 announcement covers five series: 3.10.22, 3.11.17, 3.12.15, 3.13.16, and 3.14.8 . Their version numbers look like a routine patch sweep. Their support implications are different. | Python series | Upstream status on October 5, 2026 | What that means for an upgrade | | ------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 3.10 | End of life; 3.10.22 is

The future EOL months are scheduled dates and can change. There is another distinction worth keeping straight: support status is not installer availability . Python 3.11 and 3.12 still receive upstream security fixes, but the announced 3.11.17 and 3.12.15 releases are source-only. Python 3.10.22 is also source-only, and that series is now unsupported. A missing Windows or macOS installer does not mean every series in the announcement is EOL. An available installer does not guarantee years of full maintenance ahead. docs.title: RAG vs Long Context: When Do You Actually Need Retrieval?
docs.text: RAG vs Long Context: When Do You Actually Need Retrieval?. A model with a large context window can take in a lot of material in one request. That makes it tempting to put every document you have into the prompt and call the problem solved. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) takes the opposite first step: find a small, relevant set of passages, then ask the model to use those passages. Neither approach is automatically better. They solve different problems. Long context is a way to give a model more of the input. RAG is a way to decide which input it should see, usually from a collection that is too large, too changeable, or too sensitive to send in full. The better question is not "Which one is more advanced?" It is "What information should be available for this request, and how much work should happen before the model sees it?" The distinction In a long-context design, the application assembles the relevant conversation, instructions, and documents into one prompt: The model receives that bundle directly. A larger context window lets the bundle contain more tokens, but the application still has to choose and format the material. Long context does not mean the model automatically knows where the relevant paragraph is. It only means the paragraph can fit. RAG adds a retrieval step: The index might use keyword search, vector similarity, metadata filters,

docs.title: RAG vs Long Context: When Do You Actually Need Retrieval?
docs.text: RAG vs Long Context: When Do You Actually Need Retrieval?. or a combination. The retrieved passages are evidence for one generation request. The source collection can be updated independently of the model. That makes RAG useful for private or frequently changing information. Fine-tuning is a different tool again. It changes model behavior or teaches patterns through training examples. It is generally not a substitute for making a changing knowledge base available at request time. When long context fits Use long context when the complete input is already known and reasonably sized. Consider a document review. If a user asks for a summary of one contract, loading the contract in full avoids the risk that a retrieval query misses an exception or a definition. The same applies to comparing two design documents, reviewing a pull request with a bounded diff, or extracting fields from a form whose structure is important. Long context also works well when the task depends on relationships across the whole input. A model may need to see the introduction and an appendix together, compare repeated terms, or track a decision through a sequence of meeting notes. Retrieval can return useful fragments, but it can also hide the connections between them. Long context also has operational benefits: - The request path has fewer moving parts. There is no index, embedding pipeline, or retrieval service to operate. - Debugging

docs.title: RAG vs Long Context: When Do You Actually Need Retrieval?
docs.text: RAG vs Long Context: When Do You Actually Need Retrieval?. is more direct. You can inspect the prompt and see the input the model received. - There is no retrieval recall problem for material that you deliberately included. - A small, temporary corpus does not need to be indexed before it can be used. This does not make long context free. More input usually means more tokens to process, which can increase latency and cost. Large prompts can also contain distractors. Models may give less attention to a detail surrounded by a great deal of unrelated text, even when the detail technically fits in the window. Context limits are also hard limits, so a design that works for today's document may fail when the document grows. Start with long context when the corpus for a request is bounded, the whole corpus matters, and adding retrieval would mostly add infrastructure rather than improve the answer. When RAG is worth adding RAG fits when the collection is larger than a useful prompt or when only a small part of it matters for each request. A product support assistant over many manuals, an internal search assistant over changing policies, and a coding tool for a large repository all fit this pattern. Sending the entire collection for every question is wasteful and can make the model's job harder. Retrieval narrows the evidence to passages

docs.title: RAG vs Long Context: When Do You Actually Need Retrieval?
docs.text: RAG vs Long Context: When Do You Actually Need Retrieval?. that have a plausible relationship to the question. RAG is also a good fit when knowledge changes more often than the model or application is deployed. Updating a document and its index can be a faster operational path than retraining a model or rebuilding a huge prompt at request time. It can also help enforce boundaries: retrieve only documents the requesting user is allowed to see, rather than placing an entire private corpus in a shared prompt assembly step. RAG shifts correctness into the retrieval pipeline. A fluent answer based on the wrong passages is still wrong. Common failure modes include: - The relevant passage may not have been indexed, may have been split poorly, or may not have ranked highly enough. - The user's wording may differ from the words in the source, and vector or keyword search alone may miss it. - A chunk may omit the heading, table context, or definition needed to interpret it. - Stale and current documents may both be retrieved without a clear precedence rule. - Retrieval may ignore document or row-level authorization. RAG is more than "add a vector database." It is a search system with a generation step attached. Search quality, freshness, permissions, and observability deserve the same attention as the model call. A decision framework Ask these questions before choosing

docs.text: RAG vs Long Context: When Do You Actually Need Retrieval?. an architecture. 1. What is the corpus for one request? Count the material the model genuinely needs, not every file that exists. If it is a single document, a bounded set of records, or a small diff, long context usually fits well. If it is a large repository or a growing document collection, retrieval is more likely to pay off. Estimate the worst case, not just the average. A prompt that fits most of the time but overflows on the largest customer account needs a defined behavior for that account. 2. Does the whole corpus matter? If the answer requires global comparison, ordering, or reconciliation, include the complete relevant input or use a staged process that preserves those relationships. If each question usually concerns a few independent facts, retrieving those facts is more efficient. 3. How often does the information change? For stable source material, either approach may work. For information that changes daily, retrieval gives you a direct update path, provided the indexing and deletion process is reliable. docs.text: RoastTube: Let AI Roast Your YouTube Decisions and History. Your YouTube likes are a strange thing to hand to a stranger. RoastTube asks for them anyway. Sign in, let it read the videos you liked, the channels you follow, the playlists you saved, and it will score your taste and print a verdict in the voice of a tabloid court that decided before you arrived. The court of one jury of one is a joke. The pipeline behind it is not, and most of this note is about that second half: what it took to make a comedy site honest enough that Google would let it keep reading someone's account. A joke with a real pipeline A roast is assembled from four things. A read-only pass over the visitor's YouTube data. A set of computed signals. A score that is arithmetic. And a model that writes the copy. Every number on the page is computed, not generated. The signals include the ratio of Shorts to longer videos, topic entropy across categories, a late-night like count, how many likes land on the same channel compared with how many channels the visitor subscribes to, and a handful of contradictions between what someone says they are interested in and what they actually save. The model's job starts after all of that, and it is narrow: turn the numbers and a limited set
