Google's reviewer found the honest bug The first verification submission came back with three findings, which I have kept verbatim because they were precise: - The privacy policy "does not have sufficient content". - The home page is "behind a login page". - The home page "does not explain the purpose". My first instinct was to look for the gate. There was not one. Anonymous requests to the home page, the privacy page and a report all returned 200, and the demo endpoint worked without a session at all. The reviewer still read the page as a login wall, because that is what the page looked like: the loudest element went straight to Google sign-in, the demo was real but unexplained, and the product's purpose existed mostly in courtroom voice. So the fix was not to remove a gate. It was to stop hiding what was already open: - Three demo defendants (a lurker, a gremlin, and an essay hoarder) run the entire pipeline with no account, and their verdicts are cached for

The useful lesson is not about OAuth. A reviewer reads the home page the way a first-time visitor does, in a few seconds, with no prior context. If the only visible path looks like a login, the product looks like a login, no matter what the anonymous routes return. A privacy policy that cites its own source The rewrite has one rule: every section describes something the code does, and where retention is easy to get wrong, it names the line that decides it. Reports live in Workers KV under a random id and have no TTL, so the policy says a report is kept until deletion is requested, and confirms deletion within 30 days. docs.text: Senior Software Engineering Interview Questions — What Actually Gets Asked. The difference between a $150K mid-level offer and a $350K+ senior offer isn't years of experience. It's how you answer the same five categories of questions everyone else fumbles. Most candidates walk into senior loops thinking interviewers will ask them to invert binary trees. They won't. Senior interviews test something harder: how you handle ambiguity, make tradeoffs, and design systems that work in the real world. Google's senior SWE loop has a ~0.2% offer rate from initial application But candidates who prepare system design in depth instead of just memorizing Grokking pass at nearly 5x the average rate. The gap is depth, not breadth. What You'll Actually Get Asked Senior interviews cluster into four buckets. Most people over-prepare for the first and ignore the other three. That's exactly why they get down-leveled. Coding and Data Structures (The Warm-Up) At senior level, coding questions aren't about whether you can write a for-loop. They're about whether you can spot the optimal approach in 60 seconds and articulate why. 1. "Design a URL shortener." Tests hashing, base62 encoding, collision handling, and whether you ask "what's the read:write ratio?" before writing a line of code. 2. "Implement a rate limiter." Seniors go deeper than DNS + HTTP: they cover HSTS preload lists, TLS 1.3 0-RTT, TCP fast open, HTTP/3 QUIC, and how service workers intercept the request before it even hits the network. Deep Dive: How Would You Count Unique Users at Scale? This question deserves its own section because it's a great senior-level litmus test. It sounds simple, has an obvious wrong answer, and the right answer needs a genuinely clever algorithm most developers haven't heard of. The Naive Answer (That Gets You Down-Leveled) The problem? If you have 100 million unique users and each user ID is a 36-character UUID, that's roughly 3.6 GB of RAM just for user IDs. Now run this across 200 services in a microservice architecture. You've just spent $50K/month on memory for a single counter. The Senior Answer: HyperLogLog HyperLogLog is a probabilistic algorithm, invented by Philippe Flajolet in 2007, that can estimate the number of unique items in a dataset using a fixed amount of memory (typically 1.5 KB) with a standard error of about 2%. Let that sink in: 1.5 KB can count 1 billion unique items with about 2% error. What HyperLogLog gives you: Fixed memory: 1.5 KB whether you're counting

docs.text: Senior Software Engineering Interview Questions — What Actually Gets Asked. 1,000 or 1,000,000,000 unique items Constant time: O(1) per operation, always Mergeable: Combine two HLL counters by taking the max of each register. Perfect for distributed systems About 2% error: Not exact, but for "how many unique users visited today?" 2% is perfectly fine How It Works (Plain English) Imagine you flip a coin repeatedly. On average, you'll get a "heads" within 2 flips. But if I tell you someone flipped a coin and got tails 10 times before their first heads, you'd suspect they flipped the coin a lot of times. That's the core insight. HyperLogLog replaces coin flips with hash functions: 1. Hash every user ID into a random-looking 64-bit number. The hash function spreads values uniformly. A user ID like "user-1234" becomes something like 0b001011010... . 2. Look at the binary pattern. In a random stream of bits, you'd expect to see a 1 in the first position about 50% of the time. A 1 in the third position? About 12.5% of the time. So if you see a hash where the first 1 is at position 20, that's incredibly rare. It's roughly a 1-in-2²⁰ event, which means you've probably seen a lot of unique hashes. 3. Divide into registers. The hash's first few bits choose a "register" (a bucket), and the remaining bits are used to

docs.text: Senior Software Engineering Interview Questions — What Actually Gets Asked. find the position of the leftmost 1-bit. With 2¹⁴ = 16,384 registers, you get roughly 1.6% standard error. 4. Track the maximum. Each register stores the longest run of leading zeros (plus one) it's ever seen. When all registers have seen a fair number of hashes, the harmonic mean of these values gives you the cardinality estimate. 5. Apply the magic constant. Multiply by α_m ≈ 0.7213 / (1 + 1.079 / m), where m is the number of registers. This constant, roughly 0.794 for typical register counts, corrects for the bias in using the harmonic mean. This is the "magic" that makes HyperLogLog work. HashSet vs HyperLogLog — Real Numbers HashSet (100M UUIDs): ~3.6 GB per instance, O(n) memory growth HyperLogLog (any cardinality): ~1.5 KB per instance, O(1) memory forever Accuracy trade-off: 100% exact → 98% accurate, 2,400,000x less memory Merge cost: HashSets require full data transfer; HLL merges in microseconds by comparing registers HyperLogLog in 30 Lines of TypeScript Here's a minimal but functional implementation. In production you'd use a proper 64-bit hash (like MurmurHash3 or xxHash), but this captures the essence: Interview Tip When the interviewer asks "How would you count unique users at scale?", lead with HyperLogLog. The Interview Is a Conversation, Not an Interrogation The biggest mindset shift that separates senior offers from mid-level rejections: the best candidates treat the interview as a design collaboration between colleagues, not a test to be passed. They ask questions. They push back (respectfully) on constraints that don't make sense. They think out loud so the interviewer can follow their reasoning. They say "I don't know" when they don't know, and then they figure it out. Senior engineers aren't hired because they have all the answers. docs.text: STAR+R: The Behavioral Interview Framework That Lands Senior Offers (With 5 Real Stories). 87% of mid-level candidates can tell a STAR story. 12% can tell a senior one. The difference is the +R. Most engineers walk into behavioral interviews with polished STAR scripts. Clean. Tidy. Mid-level. Senior staff+ interviewers have heard that script a hundred times that day. What separates offers from rejects isn't whether you completed the project. It's whether you can articulate what you learned, what you'd do differently, and how that changed the way you operate. That's STAR+R — the difference between a competent IC and the leader they'll pay $350K+ to hire. At Google, behavioral interviews carry more weight than coding in determining level and comp A L5 candidate who nails system design but bombs behavioral gets down-leveled to L4. A candidate who tells STAR+R stories gets the staff+ panel to champion them. Why Traditional STAR Gets Down-Leveled The classic STAR format answers the question. And that's the problem. Mid-level candidates sound like they're reading a resume bullet. Senior candidates sound like they're sharing a lesson they've internalized. Interviewers at senior+ level look for four things STAR alone doesn't prove: 1. Growth velocity — Did you learn from this, or just execute? 2. The 5 Key Stories Every Senior Needs You need 5 stories in your back pocket. Not 15. Not 3. Here's what each covers. 1. A Failure You Owned Publicly The production outage you caused, owned, and fixed. It taught you about blameless culture. The best failure stories don't deflect. They start with "I made the change that took down payments for 12 minutes." Key ingredients: your specific mistake, the blast radius quantified ("3,000 failed transactions," not "some users"), the immediate fix, the systemic change you drove, and how you now approach code reviews differently. A failure without reflection is just a mistake. A failure with reflection is leadership. 2. A Conflict You Navigated The stakeholder who wanted the impossible. It's about how you turned confrontation into collaboration. Pick a real conflict with a peer or senior stakeholder. Key ingredients: what they wanted and why it seemed impossible, your first instinct (which you didn't act on), the data-backed alternative you brought, how you preserved the relationship, and how this changed your approach to pushback. 3. docs.title: System Design Patterns That Show Up In Every Senior Interview (With Diagrams & Math)
docs.text: System Design Patterns That Show Up In Every Senior Interview (With Diagrams & Math). Most candidates fail system design rounds not because they don't know the patterns, but because they mix up CAP, sharding, and replication under pressure. I wrote this cheatsheet to fix that. System design interviews don't test whether you've memorized Grokking. They test whether you can pick the right pattern for the constraint and articulate why the alternatives would burn down production at 3 AM. Here are the 12 patterns that appear in every senior loop, with the math and tradeoffs that actually matter. Google, Meta, and Netflix all share the same ~15 system design patterns A 2024 internal study found that 73% of senior candidates could name them, and only 12% could correctly identify when each one breaks. The interview is about edge cases, not flashcards. The 12 Patterns That Keep Systems Alive 1. Load Balancing — L4 vs L7 Load balancers sit in front of your servers and distribute traffic. L4 (Layer 4) works at the transport layer (TCP/UDP). It's fast, doesn't inspect payloads, and routes by IP + port. L7 (Layer 7) inspects HTTP headers, cookies, and paths. It's slower but smarter. Algorithms: Round-robin (simple), least connections (respects load), consistent hashing (session affinity). Use L4 for internal load balancing (lower latency) and L7 at the edge for path-based routing. L7 is also where you configure rate limiting. Your

Caching — Four Patterns, One Invocation Tax | Pattern | Read Perf | Write Perf | Staleness Risk | Use Case | | ----------------- | -------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------- | -------------------- | | Cache-aside | Miss → load to cache | Write DB, invalidate cache | Low | Most APIs | | Write-through | Fast | Write DB + cache together | None (sync) | Consistency-critical | | Write-behind | Fast | Write cache, async flush DB | High (crash = loss) | High-write, low-CR | | Refresh-ahead | Pre-warmed | — | Predictable | ML model predictions | The cache invalidation tax: every caching strategy trades consistency for speed. Twitter's timeline cache invalidates on every tweet. Netflix's CDN cache invalidates only on re-encoding. Know which tradeoff you're making. 3. CDN — Edge Caching at Scale Content Delivery Networks sit PoPs globally and cache static (and dynamic) content. Cache key design is everything: include Accept-Encoding for compression-aware caching, strip session cookies to avoid cache fragmentation. Purge strategies: TTL-based (set it and forget it, but stale during window), purge-by-tag (Cloudflare tiered cache, instant but expensive), and versioned URLs ( bundle.a1b2c3.js ). Safest but hardest to implement. 4. Message Queues — Log vs Queue Two fundamentally different models: Kafka (log-based): Durable,

Great for event streaming, audit logs, and replaying after a bug fix. RabbitMQ / SQS (queue-based): Ephemeral, at-most-once or at-least-once delivery. Messages get deleted after ack. No replay. Great for task dispatch, decoupling services, and workloads where ordering is unnecessary. Kafka's durability costs matter. Size partitions carefully. Too few and consumers starve. Too many and rebalancing takes 30+ seconds. RabbitMQ handles ~50K queues easily. Kafka struggles past 10K topics. Different ceilings. 5. Sharding — Splitting Data Across Nodes Three approaches, each with a distinct pain point: - Hash sharding: shard = hash(key) % N . Simple, even distribution. But adding a node reshuffles everything, hence consistent hashing. - Range sharding: Data split by key ranges (A–D, E–H). Great for range queries. But hot spots are inevitable (all new users land in one shard). - Geographic sharding: Data local to users per region. Great latency, but cross-region queries and failover are painful. The rebalancing pain: Resharding a 10TB database means moving terabytes across a network. That means hours of double capacity or degraded reads. YouTube shards by channel_id hash and rebalances gradually, one shard at a time. 6. Consistent Hashing — Why Cache Clusters Survive Traditional hash sharding breaks when nodes change. Consistent hashing places nodes and

When a node goes down, only its keys move, not every key in the cluster. Virtual nodes solve the hot-node problem: each physical node pretends to be 50–200 virtual nodes scattered around the ring. Small clusters get even distribution without manual shard assignment. Used by: Amazon Dynamo, Discord, Cassandra, and most CDN cache tiers. 7. Replication — Leader, Multi-Leader, Leaderless | Model | Writes | Reads | Consistency | Survivability | | ----------------------- | ----------- | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | | Leader-follower | Single node | Any replica | Eventual (sync writes optional) | Leader failure = failover | | Multi-leader | Any leader | Any replica | Conflict resolution needed (CRDTs / last-write-wins) | N nodes survive N–1 failures | | Leaderless (Dynamo) | Quorum W | Quorum R | Tunable (W+R > N) | N nodes survive N–min(W,R) failures | Dynamo-style quorum: With N=3, W=2 writes, R=2 reads, you tolerate 1 node failure without losing consistency. The tradeoff? Stale data if W+R Don't say "we need CP." Say "we need CP during partitions, but in steady state we use AP with read-after-write consistency in the same AZ." That's how DynamoDB actually works, and it's a much more interesting answer. 9.

CQRS — Separate Read and Write Models Command Query Responsibility Segregation means your write model (commands) and read model (queries) are different data structures. Writes use a normalized relational model for transactional integrity. Reads use denormalized projections for fast queries. When it makes sense: Complex domains where reads and writes have different shapes. Greg Young's banking example: deposits (writes) use one validation flow; balance queries (reads) aggregate from a materialized view. When it doesn't: Simple CRUD apps with equal read/write ratio. You're just adding complexity for no benefit. 10. Event Sourcing — The Log as Source of Truth Instead of storing the current state, store every event that led to it. The current state is a projection, a fold over the event stream. User changed email from X to Y on Tuesday? That's an event. Account locked? That's an event. Projections are materialized views rebuilt by replaying the event log. Need a new read model? Replay from the beginning. Bug in billing code? Fix the projection and replay. Only use event sourcing when you genuinely need the event log: financial audits, compliance, collaborative editing (CRDTs). If you just need current state, use a normal database. Storage grows forever, rebuilding projections is slow, and event schema evolution hurts. 11. Microservices vs Modular Monolith Microservices buy you independent deployability and team autonomy,

Modular monoliths keep the deployment simplicity of a single app while enforcing module boundaries at compile time (Java modules, Go packages, Rust crates). Start as a modular monolith. Extract services when you have a proven performance bottleneck or a team boundary that genuinely needs independent deploys. Shopify ran as a monolith handling 1M+ RPM. You don't need microservices until you need microservices. 12. Idempotency Keys — The Payment Anti-Disaster Pattern A unique token (UUID) sent with a request. The server checks if it's already processed the key. If yes, return cached result. If no, process and store. Why this matters: Payment gateways, webhooks, and retry logic would otherwise double-charge customers or fire duplicate events. Stripe requires an Idempotency-Key header on every mutating request. TTL matters: 24 hours is typical. Keys must be unique per operation. Reuse a key across operations and you'll silently skip the new one. This signals senior-level thinking right away. Worked Example: URL Shortener Every senior interview has a URL shortener problem. Here's a 4-step framework. Step 1: Requirements and Capacity: - 100M new URLs/month → 40 QPS writes - 10:1 read/write → 400 QPS reads, peak 1200 QPS - ~100GB/month raw storage → ~6TB at 5 years Step 2: API Design: Step 3: Data Model (PostgreSQL): Short code generation: Base62 encoding (a–z, A–Z, 0–9) of a random 7-byte value. 62^7 = ~3.5 trillion combinations. That's plenty of headroom. Step 4: Redirect Flow (Cache-Aside): Analytics: Write click events to a Kafka topic, batch-process every 5 minutes, update click_count . Don't increment per request, or you'll swamp the DB at 1200 QPS. Abuse prevention: Rate-limit creation per IP (10 URLs/min). Check against a bloom filter of known spam domains. Candidates who nail this ask: "Is our read-to-write ratio 10:1 or 100:1?" docs.title: What Happens to the Economy When Tech Companies Mass Lay Off Workers?
docs.text: What Happens to the Economy When Tech Companies Mass Lay Off Workers?. Between 2022 and May 2026, public layoff trackers count more than 820,000 tech jobs cut across companies like Meta, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and hundreds of startups. The peak was 2023, with roughly 264,000 tracked layoffs. 2024 cooled but still saw about 153,000 cuts, 2025 added roughly 125,000, and 2026 had already crossed six figures by late May. This wasn't routine restructuring -- it was a sector-wide reset after a decade of overhiring fueled by near-zero interest rates. If you're a developer, you felt it. Job postings dried up. Offer rescissions became normalized. Senior engineers competed for mid-level roles. But beyond the personal anxiety, what does this actually do to the broader economy? Why Tech Layoffs Hit Differently Not all layoffs are equal. A wave of retail layoffs affects the economy differently than a wave of tech layoffs. Here's why tech workers are economically disproportionate: High income, high spending multiplier. The average software engineer in the US earns $130,000–$220,000. Economists use a concept called the local multiplier effect — each high-paying tech job creates an estimated 4–5 additional local service jobs (restaurants, childcare, construction, retail). When that tech job disappears, those 4–5 downstream jobs are at risk too. Concentrated geography. This concentration amplifies local impacts. High equity exposure. Unlike most workers, many tech employees have significant wealth tied to stock options and RSUs. When layoffs happen alongside stock price drops — which is common since layoffs often signal broader company stress — employees lose both income and paper wealth simultaneously. The Housing Market Effect This is the most visible and measurable economic impact. Let's look at what happened in San Francisco after the 2022–2023 tech layoff wave: - Office vacancy rates in SF hit 36% in 2024 — the highest of any major US city - Median rents in SoMa and SOMA-adjacent neighborhoods fell 15–20% from 2022 peaks - Commercial real estate values in tech-heavy corridors dropped 40–60% The mechanism: high-earning tech workers competed for premium housing and drove up prices. Their departure — or their employers' collapse — removes this demand. In cities where tech is the dominant employer, this can trigger a downward spiral : lower property values → lower property tax revenue → municipal budget cuts → degraded public services → further exodus. For context: the U.S. tech workforce is under 10 million people nationally, but the spending is highly concentrated in metro areas. Their layoffs don't just reduce aggregate demand -- they hollow out specific local economies. Consumer Spending and the Confidence Effect Aggregate demand drives economies. When thousands of $150K+ earners lose their jobs, the direct spending reduction is significant. But the indirect confidence effect is larger. Economists distinguish between two types of consumer behavior: - Current income effect : you stop spending because you lost income - Permanent income hypothesis : you change spending based on expectations of future income Tech workers who remain employed after rounds of layoffs often significantly reduce discretionary spending — not because they can't afford it, but because they're uncertain whether their job is next. This behavioral shift is hard to measure but matters enormously. After large 2022-2024 layoff rounds, the pullback showed up in categories that depend on high-income confidence: - Restaurant and entertainment spending - Large discretionary purchases like cars, furniture, and travel - Home improvement and renovation work - Premium subscriptions and business software bought by small teams Multiply this across hundreds of thousands of workers who survived layoffs but changed their behavior, and you get a measurable drag on consumer-driven economic sectors. docs.text: What Happens to the Economy When Tech Companies Mass Lay Off Workers?. The startup ecosystem is where the economy regenerates tech capacity. Layoffs affect it in complex, contradictory ways. The talent availability paradox. On one hand, layoffs flood the market with experienced engineers, making talent more accessible and affordable for startups. Founders who had struggled to recruit senior engineers during the 2021 boom suddenly had more realistic hiring conversations. This is genuinely good for startups trying to build. On the other hand, consumer-facing startups face destroyed demand . B2C startups targeting tech workers — fintech apps, premium productivity tools, high-end consumer software — see their addressable market shrink directly when their core customer base loses jobs or cuts spending. The venture capital feedback loop. VC funding and tech employment are deeply correlated. When tech companies cut costs and signal market contraction, VCs tighten their own portfolios. Sequoia's famous "Adapt or Die" memo in 2022 explicitly told portfolio companies to cut burn rates, which cascaded into thousands of startup layoffs beyond the big-tech ones. Less VC funding → fewer new companies → fewer new jobs created to absorb laid-off workers. The founder opportunity. There is a silver lining that economists and VCs frequently note: recessions and downturns create the best companies . The 2022–2024 layoff wave has already spawned thousands of new AI-focused startups, many founded by ex-FAANG engineers. The Structural Shift: AI as the Real Variable Here's what makes the current layoff cycle different from all previous ones: the stated reason for many cuts is AI-driven productivity gains , not just economic cycles. When large tech companies cite AI investment, efficiency, and flatter organizations as reasons for headcount reductions, they're signaling something the 2008 or 2001 cycles didn't involve -- that some of these jobs may not come back, even during the next economic expansion. The economic implications of this are significant and contested: Scenario A: Augmentation (optimistic). AI tools make each developer 2–3x more productive. Companies need fewer developers for the same output, but the economy grows faster because software gets built cheaper and faster. GDP grows. Employment shifts — fewer developers, more AI trainers, more product managers, more security specialists. Scenario B: Displacement (pessimistic). AI automates entire job categories faster than new categories emerge. Unlike previous technological shifts (the internet, mobile), AI substitution happens across white-collar work simultaneously. The transition period creates prolonged unemployment and economic dislocation. This is a distributional problem — the economy may grow while tech employment stays flat or contracts. The Government Revenue Problem This is underappreciated in most layoff analyses. Tech workers pay significantly more in income tax than the average worker — not just because of salaries, but because of capital gains from RSU and stock option vesting. During the 2020-2021 tech boom, California collected record income tax revenue, much of it from IPO-related capital gains and stock compensation. When financial markets cooled and layoffs began in 2022, California's revenue base weakened sharply. The Legislative Analyst's Office later estimated a $68 billion budget problem for 2024-25 , with 2022-23 revenue coming in $26 billion below budget assumptions . The state is unusually exposed to tech cycles because income-tax receipts depend heavily on high earners and capital gains. This creates a pro-cyclical government funding problem : when the economy is booming (and government spending is most needed for public goods), tech-driven tax revenue is high. When layoffs happen and unemployment services are most needed, that same tax base collapses. States with heavy tech sector dependency are essentially running a hidden leveraged bet on tech employment. What This Means for Your Career as

The 2010s model of "become a developer, get multiple competing offers, negotiate aggressively" no longer universally applies. The direction changed: fewer openings, longer interview loops, more applicants per role, and less leverage for mid-level generalist engineers. Specialization now matters more than generalism. AI can handle more generalist coding tasks. The engineers with strong job security are those with domain expertise that's hard to replicate: distributed systems at scale, security, ML infrastructure, regulatory-heavy domains (fintech/healthtech), and embedded/systems work. Geographic diversification is real. The remote work normalization accelerated by COVID — and not reversed by layoffs — has genuinely distributed tech employment. Warsaw, Bangalore, São Paulo, and Toronto now compete in the same talent market as San Francisco. This is deflationary for US tech wages but inflationary for global economic opportunity. Equity is not a salary substitute. The 2022 crash reminded thousands of engineers that unvested RSUs are not money. If you took a below-market salary for equity that never vested, that was a real economic loss. Cash compensation is worth more during uncertainty. Build financial buffer, not lifestyle inflation. The Macro Outlook If mass layoffs continue at scale — particularly AI-driven cuts across not just tech but finance, legal, healthcare administration, and other white-collar sectors — the economic consequences are severe: 1. Consumer spending contracts across premium discretionary categories 2. Housing markets in tech hubs reprice significantly downward 3. Local governments face fiscal crises from reduced tax bases 4. Inequality widens as the gains from AI productivity accrue to capital, not labor 5. But the transition is not smooth, not fast, and not evenly distributed. For developers, the message is uncomfortable but clear: the era of unconditional demand for software engineers is over . docs.text: Testing AI Agent Actions: A Runnable Approval and Retry Harness. An agent proposes a ticket. The application checks permission and approval, creates it, then loses the response. The agent retries. Does the second attempt create a second ticket? That question is small enough to test without a model. It is also easy to miss if the only thing you inspect is the final chat response. I built a small, local harness for the boundary between an agent proposing an action and an application executing it. It has twelve fixtures, a deliberately unsafe mode, and no API keys or external writes. You can download both files and run the same checks. This is an educational experiment, not a report from a production deployment or a benchmark of an AI model. It tests a deterministic action gate. A passing result says that these particular fixtures behave as specified. Run the example Download the evaluation script and test fixtures into the same directory. Read the script, then run it with Node.js: The first command should print 12/12 fixtures passed (guarded mode) and exit successfully. The second deliberately bypasses the gate. It should print 1/12 fixtures passed (unsafe mode) and exit with code 1. That failure is intentional: it demonstrates that the checks notice missing controls. Both modes write only to an in-memory array. In this repository, the equivalent command is: Separate a proposal

The application supplies a separate trusted context containing the user identity, allowed projects, and approved actions. In the fixtures, that context is test setup. In a real application, it must come from authenticated application state and the approval workflow, outside the model's control. The ordering matters. Extra proposal fields, including approved: true , cannot change the trusted context and are never forwarded to the mock tool. The twelve fixtures Each fixture starts with a fresh gate. It does not prove a model resists prompt injection. No model reads the document here. Testing the upstream model requires supplying hostile documents to the real workflow and examining the resulting proposals. A retry must preserve the identity of the work The demo scopes its request key to the user and project. When the same key arrives again, it compares the approved action with the recorded one: - Same key and same action: report a duplicate without another write. - Same key and different action: report a conflict without another write. The request key must remain stable across retries. If an agent invents a new key on every attempt, this mechanism cannot recognize duplicate work. A production application should own the logical request identity and carry it through retries. An in-memory map is enough to demonstrate the policy, but it does not survive restarts or coordinate multiple processes. This example's execution is synchronous. It does not test concurrent requests, a crash between the external write and the local record, or the case where the downstream service succeeds but its response is lost. Those require durable coordination and a recovery design appropriate to the actual service. Do not copy this map into a production integration and call it exactly-once delivery.

docs.text: Understory: Engineering Blogs, Explained, With Receipts. I read a lot of engineering blogs. Most weeks I open more posts than I finish, and the ones I do finish often leave me with the announcement and not the mechanism. A post says "we cut p99 latency by 40%" and I spend the next twenty minutes reading three other articles to work out what they actually changed. So I built Understory . It watches the posts that engineeringblogs.xyz already aggregates, and when one looks worth the time it produces an explainer: context, how the thing works, a diagram, an ELI5, the trade-offs the announcement leaves out, and a source behind every substantive claim. A person reviews each one before it goes live. Try it: understory.piyushmehta.com. Source on GitHub, code under MIT and content under CC BY 4.0. The name is the layer of a forest that sits under the canopy. The headline is the canopy. The interesting part is underneath it. What a reader gets Each explainer is written for a senior engineer at a different company who wants to use the idea in their own work. The goal is that you can explain the post's mechanism to a colleague without reading anything else first. A page has a fixed shape: - a context headline and a one-sentence summary, so you know in five seconds whether to keep

docs.text: I Moved This Site From Vercel to Cloudflare. Here Is What Broke.. This site ran on Vercel for years without much drama. Then I moved it to Cloudflare Workers, and for about a day, every link I shared to a new post rendered as a blank blue rectangle. Not broken in an obvious way: the request came back 200 OK , the content type was image/png , the dimensions were exactly right. There was just nothing on it. No title, no text, nothing. That single bug turned into the best possible tour of what actually changes when you move a site off a Node.js serverless platform and onto a V8 isolate. This is the record of what moved, what broke, and why. The short version: the adapter swap was the easy part. The hard part was a native Rust binary that only works at build time now, and a caching layer that kept an old broken image alive long after the underlying bug was fixed. Why leave Vercel at all Nothing was on fire. The honest reason is that I wanted one platform instead of two: Cloudflare already sat in front of DNS and a couple of other side projects, and running the actual site somewhere else meant a second dashboard, a second set of environment variables, and a second mental model for "how does a request get served." Workers also don't

None of that is a knock on Vercel. It's a genuinely good platform, and this migration was about consolidation, not escaping something broken. The adapter swap The actual config change is small. astro.config.mjs went from the Vercel adapter to the Cloudflare one: Vercel's ISR (incremental static regeneration) doesn't have a Cloudflare equivalent, so that config just disappears: pages are either prerendered at build time or served on demand from the Worker, with no middle ground where a page gets cached and silently regenerated later. A new wrangler.jsonc shows up alongside it, describing the Worker itself: the entrypoint, the assets binding, and (this detail mattered more than it looked like it would) where the static output actually lives. Where Vercel produced one build output, Cloudflare produces two: dist/client for everything Workers Assets serves directly, and dist/server for the actual Worker script. That's the right fix, and by itself it's not even a hard one. The actual bug was subtler, and it's the reason this took a day instead of an hour. The font file was being resolved with path.join(process.cwd(), 'InterVariable.ttf') , a path that happens to work when you run node from the project root and does not reliably resolve to the same place inside a build runner's working directory. When the font failed to load, the code didn't throw. It fell through to a fallback renderer that draws the card with plain SVG and no font attached, which resvg silently renders as nothing. Correct dimensions, correct content type, 200 OK , and zero visible pixels of text: a blank blue card that looks, to any monitoring you might have, like a complete success. The fix was to resolve the font relative to the module's own file instead of the process's working directory, and to give the fallback path an explicit, always-available font so it can never again silently render invisible text. docs.title: My 12TB Drive Failed. ZFS Saved 3.4TB of Data
docs.text: My 12TB Drive Failed. ZFS Saved 3.4TB of Data. One of my 12TB Seagate IronWolf drives developed 52 bad sectors. At that point, about 3.4TB of homelab data was depending on the surviving half of my ZFS mirror. The Proxmox server stayed online. My media and application data remained available, Seagate replaced the failed drive without hassle, and ZFS rebuilt the mirror onto a new 16TB IronWolf. This is the sequence I followed, including the USB enclosure reset that briefly suspended the pool and the checksum errors ZFS caught after a later reboot. ZFS could not stop the drive from failing. It did stop that failure from deleting my data. TL;DR: the recovery in numbers - Failed disk: 12TB Seagate IronWolf with 52 bad sectors - Data at risk: 3.37TiB allocated on a degraded ZFS mirror - Warranty replacement: new 16TB Seagate IronWolf - Resilver: 3.38TiB in 5 hours 30 minutes - Resilver result: zero errors and the mirror returned ONLINE - Usable capacity: still 10.9TiB because the other mirror member is 12TB The mirror supplied another copy, ZFS checked the blocks, and Seagate supplied the replacement drive. My Proxmox ZFS mirror before the failure My vault pool lives on a Proxmox server. It stores media, application configuration, and other homelab data. I built it as a two-drive ZFS mirror: Both drives sit in a TerraMaster USB DAS. The

ZFS needs that direct access to manage the mirror and verify checksums. The pool held about 3.37TiB of allocated data when I replaced the drive. A mirror gets the capacity of its smallest member, with another copy of each block on the other disk. When one drive started failing, that second copy kept the pool alive. The 12TB IronWolf had 52 bad sectors SMART showed 52 bad sectors on one of the 12TB drives. I was not going to clear the warning and keep using it. Once a disk cannot reliably read its own sectors, I do not want it holding the only copy of anything. I removed it from service and opened a Seagate warranty claim. The process was painless, and Seagate honored the warranty. They sent a 16TB Seagate IronWolf to replace the failed 12TB drive. The replacement arrived with the clean baseline I wanted: Its short SMART self-test also completed without error. The Seagate part was refreshingly easy. A failed drive already gives you enough to worry about. I did not have to fight the warranty process too. The degraded mirror kept serving data After I removed the failed disk, ZFS showed the pool as DEGRADED : The warning was serious. The pool had

The disk had failed, the mirror had lost redundancy, and ZFS made both facts obvious without taking my data offline. Hot-plugging the replacement reset the USB enclosure The recovery got more stressful when I inserted the 16TB drive. The TerraMaster enclosure reset its shared USB connection, and the surviving 12TB disk disappeared for a moment. ZFS suspended the pool: That was the right response. With its only available member temporarily gone, ZFS stopped accepting I/O rather than claiming that writes had succeeded. Once both disks were visible again, I checked their model, serial, WWN, SMART state, and partition signatures. Then I resumed the pool: The pool returned to DEGRADED with the surviving member online. zpool clear removed the suspended state. It did not restore redundancy. This incident also exposed a weakness in my setup. Both mirrored disks share the same enclosure, cable, controller, and power supply. The mirror protects against one disk failing, but those shared components can still affect both drives at once. The replacement command was zpool replace The 16TB disk had to replace the missing mirror member. Adding it as another top-level vdev would have changed the pool topology instead of repairing the mirror. zpool add

I did not use /dev/sdc because Linux can assign a different device letter after a reboot or USB reconnect. ZFS partitioned the blank replacement and started resilvering it. ZFS resilvered 3.38TiB with zero errors The resilver copied the allocated data from the surviving 12TB drive to the new 16TB drive: Both drives finished online. ZFS recorded zero read, write, and checksum errors during the resilver. The datasets mounted normally, Proxmox reported the storage entries as active, and the pool had redundancy again. Usable capacity remains about 10.9TiB. The smaller member limits a mirror, so the extra space on the 16TB disk cannot be used yet. If I eventually replace the remaining 12TB drive with another 16TB or larger disk, the mirror can expand. I would rather have redundancy now than extra capacity I cannot safely use. ZFS caught 11 checksum mismatches after reboot A later Proxmox reboot imported the pool and recorded 11 checksum mismatches on the new member. The pool remained ONLINE , and applications were unaffected because the other mirror member had a valid copy. SMART passed, the reallocated, pending, and uncorrectable sector counts stayed at zero, and the interface CRC count did not increase. The kernel showed no new USB reset or I/O failure, and ZFS reported no known data errors. A full scrub began checking every allocated block. I am keeping the checksum counters until it finishes because clearing them now would discard useful evidence. If the scrub finishes cleanly and the count stays at 11, I can clear the historical device errors. If the count keeps rising, I will investigate the TerraMaster bay, USB bridge, cable, power delivery, and the replacement drive. I liked seeing ZFS do what I had set it up to do. A successful read was not enough. The bytes also had to match. What ZFS and the mirror each did The mirror and ZFS handled different parts of the failure. The mirror kept another copy The surviving disk still contained the pool after the first drive became untrustworthy. Later, when one copy failed a checksum, the mirror gave ZFS another copy to read. Checksums can detect bad data, but they cannot recreate the correct bytes. That requires redundancy or a backup. ZFS checked the data ZFS checksums data and metadata. It can tell the difference between a drive returning data and a drive returning the correct

ZFS made the failures visible DEGRADED told me the pool had lost redundancy. SUSPENDED stopped I/O when the only available member vanished during the USB reset. Neither state was pleasant, but neither hid the problem. Stable disk IDs kept me on the right drive The WWN path kept pointing to the replacement even when /dev/sda , /dev/sdb , and /dev/sdc changed after reconnects and reboots. A filesystem cannot protect you if you run the right command against the wrong disk. What I will keep doing RAID is not a backup The mirror protected me from one disk failure. It would not protect me from accidental deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, a destructive command, or corruption copied to both members. Anything irreplaceable still needs an independent backup. Run scrubs and read the result A scrub verifies data while another copy is available for repair. I care whether it repaired anything, found permanent errors, or caused a device counter to increase, not only whether the scheduled job ran. Use SMART and ZFS together SMART identified the original failing drive and gave me a hardware baseline for the replacement. The later checksum events showed why filesystem checks still matter. Replacement commands should use persistent disk IDs. Treat the enclosure as shared hardware Hot-plugging one bay reset the USB path for both disks. The enclosure, USB controller, cable, and power supply need the same attention as the drives. Check the pool topology before changing it zpool replace repairs a missing mirror member. zpool add changes the topology. I checked the command and target before pressing Enter. Frequently asked questions Can ZFS recover from a failed drive? Yes, if the pool still has a valid copy. One member of my two-disk mirror failed, while the other kept the pool available. I replaced the missing member and ZFS resilvered the allocated data onto it. A single-disk ZFS pool can detect corruption with checksums, but it has no second copy to repair from. Is a ZFS mirror the same as RAID 1? Both provide two-copy redundancy. ZFS also manages the filesystem, block checksums, scrubs, repairs, snapshots, and the pool itself. When two copies disagree, ZFS can verify which one matches the stored checksum and repair the other. Does a 12TB + 16TB ZFS mirror provide 28TB? No. The smallest member limits the mirror. My 12TB + 16TB mirror remains about 10.9TiB usable. Replacing the remaining 12TB disk with another 16TB

docs.text: My 12TB Drive Failed. ZFS Saved 3.4TB of Data. or larger drive will allow the mirror to expand. Does ZFS or RAID replace a backup? No. My mirror handled one disk failure. It cannot protect both copies from deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, or a destructive command. Irreplaceable data still needs an independent backup. Should I use zpool add when replacing a failed mirror disk? No. zpool add changes the pool topology. Use zpool replace with the missing vdev and the replacement disk's stable /dev/disk/by-id/ path. The recovery was boring, which is what I wanted The working sequence was straightforward: 1. identify the failing disk; 2. keep the degraded pool stable; 3. get the warranty replacement; 4. verify its identity and SMART baseline; 5. replace the missing vdev by stable ID; 6. monitor the resilver until it finishes; and 7. check the pool, datasets, mounts, and disk health afterward. Seagate honored the warranty without hassle. ZFS and the mirror kept the drive failure from becoming a data-loss event. The drive failed, I replaced it, and my data stayed put. That is what I wanted when I built the mirror.
